scope: Nine maintained black-box optimization concepts; ongoing discovery, no saturation or scientific approval inferred.

entries.name: Predictive entropy search for multi-objective Bayesian optimization
entries.definition: A Bayesian multi-objective optimization algorithm that selects evaluations using an approximate information gain about the Pareto set, computed from sampled finite Pareto-set approximations and objective-factorized Gaussian expectation-propagation approximations to conditional predictions.

definition_evidence.locator: Sections2–2.1, PDFpp.2–4, Eqs1–8 and sampling/EP descriptions.

entries.identity_notes: This is the original PESMO procedure for information about a Pareto set under the stated independent objective models, finite sampled Pareto-set representation and EP approximations. Scalar PES targets one optimizer location; PESC adds feasibility to a scalar objective. Neither defines the multi-objective dominance factors or approximate objective-wise information allocation of PESMO. The proposed PESMOC, PPESMOC and PPES records preserve their different constrained or joint-batch targets.

claims.statement: PESMO targets information about the Pareto set in input space for several objectives, using minimization conventions. A point dominates another when it is no worse in every objective and strictly better in at least one; the Pareto set contains the nondominated points. Assume a well-defined posterior over nonempty Pareto sets and finite mutual information. At fixed surrogate hyperparameters, the ideal acquisition is I(X_star; y(x) | D), equivalently the predictive entropy of the objective observations minus their expected conditional entropy given the Pareto set. This is a target for approximation; it is not information about only a scalar optimum value or a chosen scalarization.

evidence.locator: Section1, PDFp.1 dominance definition; Section2, PDFpp.2–3, Eqs1–2. The later quantified characterization and Eq4 have the separate caveats retained below.

claims.statement: The model assigns independent Gaussian-process priors to the objectives and independent zero-mean Gaussian observation noise. At fixed independent model hyperparameters, the ordinary predictive distribution at a candidate factorizes across objectives. The reported experiments average acquisition values over sampled surrogate hyperparameters; such conditional averaging does not by itself compute the entropy of a hyperparameter mixture. Conditioning on a shared Pareto set need not preserve objective independence.

evidence.locator: Section2, PDFpp.2–3, assumptions before Eq1 and Eq3; Section4, PDFpp.5–6, acquisition averaging over hyperparameter samples.
Section1, PDFp.1, stated independence approximation; Section1.3, PDFp.4, tilted distribution and objective-factorized Gaussian projection.

claims.statement: To approximate the expectation over Pareto sets, sample finite random-feature linear approximations to each objective posterior, solve the resulting multi-objective problem approximately, and retain a finite representative set of nondominated locations. The paper describes a grid search and NSGA-II for higher-dimensional problems. Its choices of ten draws and fifty retained locations are reported numerical settings, not exact posterior sampling or fixed mathematical requirements of the algorithm. Finite search and set compression can omit parts of the true Pareto set.

evidence.locator: Section2, PDFp.3, random kernel features, grid/NSGA-II search and representative subset; Section2.1, PDFp.4, Monte Carlo average.

claims.statement: For each retained Pareto-set sample, replace the continuous-domain conditioning calculation by a finite set containing previous evaluation locations, the sampled Pareto locations and the candidate. Approximate each non-Gaussian comparison factor by a product of objective-specific bivariate Gaussian factors, fitted through expectation propagation. Reuse the factors independent of the candidate, while the paper updates candidate-dependent factors once. The Gaussian projection matches the retained within-objective moments and discards cross-objective dependence; it does not reproduce all moments of the joint tilted distribution or certify exact whole-domain Pareto-set conditioning.

evidence.locator: Section2.1, PDFpp.3–4, finite restriction, Eq6 Gaussian projection and candidate-factor reuse/update paragraph; printed comparison signs are qualified below.
Sections1.1 and1.3–1.4, PDFpp.2 and4–5, self exclusion, cavity/tilted distributions, objective-factorized moment projection and damping.

claims.statement: Within the factorized Gaussian approximation, the contribution of objective k is one half of the difference between log(v_k(x)+sigma_k_squared) and the sample average of log(v_k_conditional(x; X_star_sample)+sigma_k_squared). Here v denotes latent predictive variance and sigma_k_squared is the observation-noise variance; the entire log-variance difference is multiplied by one half. Summing these contributions yields the coupled acquisition. All logarithm arguments must be positive. This additive score follows the Gaussian factorization and finite sample approximation, and is not generally an exact additive decomposition of joint Pareto-set mutual information.

evidence.locator: Section2, PDFp.3, Eq3; Section2.1, PDFp.4, Eqs7–8 and paragraph adding observation-noise variance.
Section1.2, PDFp.3, final paragraph adding Gaussian observation-noise variance.

Pinned author implementation at commit 9525e612b94a3b76d5510a816d94eb2801219782, evaluate_acquisition_function_given_EP_solution, lines2994–2995 and3014–3026: supports observation-noise addition and the pre-clipping half-log variance terms only. Clipping before averaging is a separate version-specific choice retained in limitations, not asserted equivalence to the paper acquisition.

claims.statement: In the coupled setting, maximize the sum of the objective contributions to choose a location for evaluating all objectives. If objectives can be evaluated separately, maximize each objective contribution over location and select the objective/location pair with the largest resulting score. The same sampled Pareto sets link the objective-specific approximations. The displayed decoupled rule compares information scores and does not include a cost divisor; unequal evaluation costs do not turn it into a guaranteed optimal scheduler. Coupled and decoupled use are modes of this record, not separate concept identities.

evidence.locator: Section2.1, PDFp.4, Eqs7–8 and objective selection following Eq8; Section4.3, PDFp.8, separate evaluation counts and unequal training costs.

limitations: The ideal target assumes a well-defined joint posterior over objectives and Pareto sets. A bounded domain alone does not establish existence or regularity. Tied objective vectors, repeated input locations and degenerate covariance matrices require explicit handling; no general tie policy or empty-set fallback is invented here.

Main PDFp.1 gives a correct weak-plus-one-strict dominance definition, but its subsequent strict quantified characterization includes self comparisons. Main PDFp.3 Eq4 includes self pairs with Theta(0)=1 and reverses the minimization comparison direction; Eq6 on p.4 and supplement Eq8 on p.3 repeat that orientation. Supplement Eq3 on p.2 excludes self pairs. Even correctly oriented nondominated-membership factors do not require a supplied subset to equal the entire Pareto set. These printed products are not certified normalized densities or exact set-equality events.

The supplement has additional literal Gaussian-parameter inconsistencies: PDFp.1 Eq2 cross-term scaling differs from the symmetric precision entries in p.2 Eq4; Eq4 includes an M+M endpoint where the observed block has N+M variables; p.3 Eq7 mixes covariance and precision entries and does not in general construct the precision of the required marginal. The high-level Gaussian projection is curated without certifying these expressions as executable formulas.

Selective static inspection of the separately pinned July2016 author implementation supports minimization sign reversal, self-site removal and covariance block inversion. That version also rescales candidate covariances, uses a damped single candidate pass and clips each sampled contribution below zero before averaging. These are version-specific implementation choices, not an official erratum or proof of equivalence to the proceedings equations. Conditioning reduces entropy in expectation, so per-realization clipping is an additional approximation. No author code was executed.

Finite random features, approximate multi-objective optimization, finite Pareto representatives, EP factorization, limited candidate updates and hyperparameter averaging all introduce approximation. The original bounded checks in research/discovery/pesmo-boundaries.py illustrate selected source and information boundaries only; they do not validate full PESMO inference or its empirical accuracy.

The paper gives linear dependence on the number of objectives only for specified EP/variance linear-algebra operations with other sizes and iteration/sample budgets held fixed. Pareto-set size, input dimension, posterior sampling and acquisition maximization can dominate cost. No universal runtime improvement, convergence guarantee or benchmark reproduction is asserted.

entries.name: Predictive entropy search for multi-objective Bayesian optimization with constraints
entries.definition: A Bayesian optimization algorithm for multiple objectives and unknown constraints that selects evaluations using approximate information gain about the feasible Pareto set, estimated through sampled feasible Pareto representatives and task-factorized Gaussian expectation propagation.

definition_evidence.locator: Sections2.2–2.4, institutional PDFpp.11–20, ideal feasible-Pareto information target, sampling and EP approximation.

claims.statement: PESMOC selects evaluations to learn the Pareto set in input space for multiple objectives under unknown inequality constraints. In the source minimization convention, a point is feasible when every constraint c_j(x) is nonnegative; a feasible point dominates another when it is no worse in all objectives and strictly better in at least one. Assume a well-defined posterior over attained, nonempty feasible Pareto sets and finite mutual information, with ties handled explicitly. At fixed surrogate hyperparameters the ideal acquisition is I(X_star; y(x) | D), equivalently predictive entropy minus its expected value conditional on the feasible Pareto set. The implemented score approximates this target; it is not entropy of only the Pareto front or a scalar optimum value.

evidence.locator: Section1, institutional PDFpp.6–7 (printedpp.5–6), Eq1 and weak-plus-one-strict dominance definition; Section2.2, PDFpp.11–13, Eqs4–6. Subsequent strict quantified characterization is qualified below.

claims.statement: The method models each objective and each constraint with an independent Gaussian process and Gaussian observation noise. Conditional on fixed independent model hyperparameters, the ordinary predictive distribution factors over the objective and constraint tasks. Conditioning all tasks on a shared feasible Pareto set generally introduces dependence, which the later Gaussian projection does not retain across tasks. Averaging conditional acquisition values over sampled hyperparameters is also an approximation, rather than the entropy of the resulting predictive mixture.

evidence.locator: SectionII, PDFp.2, independent GP priors and zero-mean Gaussian noise.
Section2.2, PDFp.12, Eq5 and noise paragraph; Section4, PDFp.33, acquisition averaging over sampled hyperparameters.

claims.statement: Approximate the expectation over Pareto sets by sampling random-feature approximations to both objective and constraint posteriors. For each draw, search candidate locations, discard locations violating a sampled constraint, and retain a finite representation of the nondominated feasible locations. The paper uses a grid and discusses evolutionary search for higher dimensions. Finite features, finite search and compression of the Pareto set make these approximate samples. The paper does not specify a general acquisition policy for posterior draws with no feasible solution; relaxing a reported recommendation threshold is a separate operation.

evidence.locator: Section2.2, PDFp.14, random-feature sampling, grid search and feasibility filtering; Section2.5, PDFp.22, finite Pareto representatives; Section4, PDFp.33, separate recommendation-threshold relaxation.

claims.statement: For a retained feasible Pareto-set sample, approximate the conditioning calculation on the union of sampled Pareto locations, previous evaluation locations and the candidate. Feasibility factors constrain sampled Pareto locations; comparison factors couple objective comparisons with feasibility of competing locations. Expectation propagation replaces these non-Gaussian factors by task-specific Gaussian factors: univariate constraint factors and bivariate within-objective factors for location pairs. Reuse the factors independent of the candidate and update candidate-dependent factors once in the stated approximation. This projection discards cross-task dependence and is not exact whole-domain feasible Pareto-set conditioning.

evidence.locator: Sections2.3–2.4, PDFpp.14–17, Eqs8–14 and finite restriction/reuse paragraphs; literal self-pair and constraint-location caveats are retained below.
Sections1–4, PDFpp.3–20, cavity, tilted moments, task-factorized sites and Gaussian reconstruction; Section4.4, PDFpp.21–23, candidate computation.

claims.statement: Within the factorized Gaussian approximation, each task contributes one half of its ordinary log predictive observation variance minus the sample average of its conditional log predictive observation variance. Add that task’s observation-noise variance to the latent variance in both terms and require positive logarithm arguments. Summing over objective and constraint tasks gives the coupled score. The common factor one half follows Gaussian entropy; the main acquisition display omits it, which preserves uncosted rankings but not numerical information units. Task additivity belongs to the approximation and is not generally an exact decomposition of joint feasible-Pareto mutual information.

evidence.locator: Section2.4, PDFpp.18–19, Eqs15–18 and Gaussian-noise paragraph, read with Eq7 on PDFp.13 and the coefficient/index caveats below.
Section4.4, PDFpp.21–23, Eq54 and final noise-variance paragraph.

Pinned author implementation at commit fa54faf5b5d2e85878a1d20345898dcc0babcb80, evaluate_acquisition_function_given_EP_solution, lines6304–6308 and6331–6346: supports objective/constraint noise addition and the pre-clipping half-log variance terms only. Clipping before averaging is a separate version-specific choice retained in limitations, not asserted equivalence to the paper acquisition.

claims.statement: In coupled use, maximize the sum of task contributions to choose one location for evaluating all objectives and constraints. When tasks can be evaluated separately, maximize their individual approximate contributions and compare the maxima to select a task and location. Coupled and decoupled selection are modes of PESMOC. The displayed comparison contains no evaluation-cost divisor and does not guarantee an optimal scheduler or lower wall-clock cost when task costs differ. Multi-location parallel batch selection requires a separate acquisition construction.

evidence.locator: Section2.4, PDFpp.18–20, Eqs16–18 and selection paragraphs; Section5, PDFpp.63–64, comparison of individual acquisitions.
SectionIV, PDFp.6, parallel batch extension identified as future work.

entries.identity_notes: PESMOC targets a feasible Pareto set through objective dominance and constraint-feasibility factors. This differs from unconstrained PESMO and from scalar PESC even though the methods share approximate predictive-entropy reasoning. The single-query mechanism is distinct from the joint-batch covariance construction of PPESMOC. Version-specific paper, appendix and implementation limitations remain explicit.
limitations: Existence and measurability of the feasible Pareto target require assumptions beyond boundedness of the input domain. Distinguish no observed feasible incumbent, no feasible grid point in an approximate search, and a posterior function draw whose feasible region is empty. The paper’s recommendation relaxation on PDFp.33 is not a specified posterior-empty-draw acquisition policy. Per-constraint probability thresholds also do not imply the same simultaneous feasibility probability.

The 2019 institutional author manuscript is dated May3,2019 and has a visible gap from printedp.8 to printedp.10; the separate official supplement is dated May13,2019. The six-page September2016 arXivv2 is an earlier version. No claim of reading the inaccessible final publisher layout or the missing page is made; relevant accessible methods and the earlier independent-prior assumptions are cited explicitly.

Main Eq8 on PDFp.15 includes self comparisons with Theta(0)=1, making the literal product zero for any nonempty feasible supplied set; removing self comparisons still requires tie handling and does not make nondominated-membership factors enforce equality to the complete Pareto set. Eq10 has the minimization comparison orientation stated in the main text. The prose saying that every supplied Pareto point dominates each other point is too strong: being better in one objective does not imply dominance.

Main PDFp.17 Eq13 and supplement PDFp.9 Eq15 place constraint factors at the sampled Pareto location although their exact comparison factors depend on competitor feasibility. Main Eq7 lacks a half coefficient on the constraint log-variance terms; Eq15 lacks a common half coefficient; Eqs17–18 bind task indices instead of the Pareto-sample index in the expectation. These displays are not certified literal executable formulas.

The supplement contains further algebraic and notation defects, including the feasibility log-normalizer curvature in PDFp.12 Eq22, the observation-first difference orientation in PDFp.15 Eq30, exponential grouping in PDFpp.16–17 Eqs40/43, singular difference-Hessian inverses in PDFp.18 Eqs45–48, and covariance/precision mixing in PDFp.22 Eq61. The same section first describes a precision diagonal as a variance and then gives an inverse diagonal on p.23. Its damping prose on p.24 ends with non-positive definiteness as the stopping state. The record preserves the supported EP mechanism without claiming a complete repaired implementation or guaranteed convergence.

Selective inspection of a separately pinned May2020 author implementation provides context, not an official erratum: it uses competitor constraint values, a minimization sign, zeroed self sites, half-log entropy differences and inverse precision construction. It also caps retained observations, changes candidate covariance, damps one candidate pass, and clips sampled task scores before averaging. The empty-sample and numerical safeguards are version-specific. No author code was executed, and no equivalence to every paper equation is asserted.

Finite features, approximate search, finite Pareto representatives, EP factorization, limited candidate updates and hyperparameter averaging introduce approximation. The original bounded checks in research/discovery/pesmoc-boundaries.py establish selected finite and Gaussian counterexamples only; they are not a PESMOC implementation, empirical validation, efficiency claim or universal convergence proof.

entries.name: Parallel predictive entropy search for multi-objective Bayesian optimization with constraints
entries.definition: A batch Bayesian optimization algorithm for multiple objectives and unknown constraints that jointly selects parallel evaluation locations using approximate information gain about the feasible Pareto set, computed from sampled Pareto representatives and Gaussian EP conditional batch covariance log determinants.

definition_evidence.locator: Sections3.2–3.4, institutional PDFpp.13–16 / printedpp.12–15, joint feasible-Pareto information target, finite sampling, EP and batch log determinants.

claims.statement: PPESMOC selects a batch X of B input locations for parallel evaluations of multiple objectives and unknown constraints. In the source minimization convention, feasibility requires c_j(x) >= 0 for every constraint, and dominance means no worse in every objective and strictly better in at least one. Its ideal target is I(X_star; Y_X | D), information about the feasible Pareto set in input space from the joint observation matrix of the whole batch. Assume a well-defined posterior over attained, nonempty feasible Pareto sets, explicit tie handling and finite mutual information. By mutual-information symmetry, this equals joint predictive entropy minus its expected value conditional on the Pareto set; the practical acquisition approximates this target.

evidence.locator: Section2, institutional PDFp.5 / printedp.4, Eq1 and weak-plus-one-strict dominance definition; Section3.2, PDFp.13 / printedp.12, Eqs9–10. The later strict characterization requires the self/tie qualifications below.

claims.statement: Model each objective and constraint with an independent Gaussian process and Gaussian observation noise. At fixed hyperparameters, each task provides a B-dimensional predictive distribution with a full covariance matrix across the batch. Independence across tasks does not mean independence across batch locations. The ordinary joint entropy is a sum of taskwise Gaussian log determinants, with observation-noise covariance included. Conditioning on a shared feasible Pareto set generally couples tasks; the subsequent EP approximation discards that cross-task dependence while retaining within-task batch covariance.

evidence.locator: Section2.1, PDFp.10 / printedp.9, Eq4 and independent-GP paragraph; Sections3.2–3.3, PDFpp.13–15 / printedpp.12–14, Eqs10–15. Eq11 has the missing-log caveat below.

claims.statement: Approximate the expectation over feasible Pareto sets with samples constructed from random-feature approximations to the objective and constraint GP posteriors. Solve each sampled constrained multi-objective problem approximately and retain a finite representation of its feasible nondominated locations. The journal manuscript describes a grid of 1000 times the input dimension and at most 50 retained Pareto points; these are reported approximation choices, not exact whole-domain sampling. A failed finite search and a posterior draw with no feasible solution are distinct cases; the inspected method does not specify a general acquisition policy for either.

evidence.locator: Section3.2, PDFp.14 / printedp.13, paragraph after Eq11; Section3.3, PDFp.15 / printedp.14, finite domain restriction.

claims.statement: Restrict the conditioning calculation to previous evaluation locations, the sampled Pareto representatives and all candidate batch locations. Use feasibility factors for Pareto representatives and factors coupling competitor feasibility with objective comparisons. EP projects these onto univariate constraint factors and bivariate factors within each objective for pairs of locations. Reuse the fitted sites for observations and Pareto representatives, and refine candidate-batch sites once for each acquisition evaluation. The resulting proper Gaussian approximation supplies each task’s conditional batch covariance. Finite sites and taskwise projection do not implement exact feasible Pareto-set conditioning.

evidence.locator: Sections3.3–3.4, PDFpp.14–15 / printedpp.13–14, Eqs13–16 and finite restriction/reuse paragraphs.
Section1, PDFp.1, cached observation/Pareto factors and one candidate pass; Sections2.1–2.6, PDFpp.2–9, EP structure and covariance reconstruction, with formula caveats below.

claims.statement: For positive-definite ordinary and approximate conditional observation covariances, score a batch by one half of the sum over tasks of log det Sigma_task(X), minus one half of the Monte Carlo average of the corresponding sums of log det Sigma_task(X | X_star_sample). Include each task’s observation noise in both covariance terms. These are B-by-B determinants, not sums of independent single-location acquisitions; at B = 1 they reduce to log-variance terms. Permuting batch locations and all corresponding matrix indices leaves this score unchanged. The printed Eq16 omits the common one half, preserving its uncosted maximizers but doubling Gaussian information units. Task additivity is an approximation and does not make location scores additive.

evidence.locator: Sections3.2–3.4, PDFpp.13–16 / printedpp.12–15, Eqs10–11 and16, Gaussian-noise paragraph and permutation-symmetry discussion; common coefficient and index caveats below.
Section2.4, PDFp.8, covariance matrix at the new batch.

claims.statement: Optimize the approximate acquisition jointly over the B times input dimension coordinates of the batch. The reported procedure uses automatic differentiation and L-BFGS, with previously fitted EP sites reused and candidate sites refined once. These are derivatives of the chosen numerical approximation, not certified derivatives of exact mutual information, and local optimization does not guarantee a global best batch. This joint construction differs from repeatedly applying single-query PESMOC with hallucinated pending outcomes. The paper also describes task-specific batch scores for decoupled evaluation but explicitly leaves their empirical assessment for future work.

evidence.locator: Section2.2, PDFpp.10–11 / printedpp.9–10, fantasy baseline and batch dimensionality; Sections3.4 and4, PDFpp.15–16 and19–20 / printedpp.14–15 and18–19, joint optimization and PESMOC distinction.
Section1, PDFp.1, random initialization, Autograd, L-BFGS, maximum100 iterations and factor-reuse convention.

entries.identity_notes: PPESMOC is a joint-batch information construction for a constrained Pareto set, retaining batch covariance terms within its stated approximations. It is not independent repetition or summation of the single-query PESMOC acquisition. It also differs from single-objective PPES and from PESC-F, which schedules inexpensive acquisition updates rather than defining this joint multi-objective batch information target.
limitations: A bounded input domain alone does not ensure an attained, nonempty measurable feasible Pareto target. Distinguish absence of an observed feasible point, failure of a finite feasible-point search and an empty feasible region in a posterior function draw. The inspected primary method does not supply a general failure or empty-draw convention. Pareto ties and self comparisons require explicit treatment.

The journal source is an institutional author manuscript with a cover plus printedpp.1–28, associated with the2023 publication DOI10.1016/j.eswa.2022.119328. The official publisher supplement is separately pinned. The two-author arXivv2 dated July1,2021 is an earlier version; it is not the three-author journal layout. The inaccessible publisher main layout and external author code are not claimed as inspected or executed.

Main PDFp.13 incorrectly describes the observation vector as K+J dimensional rather than B(K+J); Eq11 on PDFp.14 omits log on constraint determinants, while Eq16 on PDFp.15 omits the common one half and uses k inside constraint sums indexed by j. The descriptive PESMO Eq8 on PDFp.12 is malformed. The record uses the supported Gaussian entropy construction without certifying those literal displays.

Main Eq12 on PDFp.14 omits the normalization needed for conditional distributions. With Theta(0)=1, Eq13 includes self comparisons and annihilates every nonempty feasible supplied set; removing self comparisons still requires tie handling and does not enforce equality to the complete Pareto set. The nearby prose also confuses non-domination with dominance. These are source caveats, not an asserted author-issued erratum or a complete repaired EP implementation.

The supplement contains algebraic and notation defects: Eq7 on p.3 gives zero feasibility log-normalizer curvature at zero instead of minus2/pi for unit cavity variance; Eq12 on p.5 reverses the minimizing difference for the declared observation-first ordering; Eqs22 and25 place logarithmic terms outside exponentials; Eqs27–30 on p.6 invert a rank-one difference Hessian product; Eq35 on p.8 has inconsistent N versus N+M block bounds; p.9 describes a damping loop ending with non-positive definite covariance. Literal execution of these equations is not validated, and convergence is not guaranteed.

Random features, finite feasible searches and Pareto representations, EP projection, one candidate-site pass, local acquisition optimization and sampled hyperparameters introduce approximation. Averaging fixed-hyperparameter information scores is not generally entropy of the predictive mixture. Duplicate noiseless latent evaluations can make covariance determinants singular; independent observation noise can make repeated evaluations informative. The source’s plotted diversity behavior is not a universal prohibition on repeated locations.

The original bounded checks in research/discovery/ppesmoc-boundaries.py concern rational covariance matrices, finite information channels and selected source-formula counterexamples. They are not GP training, full EP inference, author-code execution, a numerical benchmark or independent scientific approval. No universal runtime, approximation-accuracy, convergence, optimal-scheduling or superiority claim is made.

entries.name: Parallel predictive entropy search
entries.definition: A batch Bayesian optimization algorithm that jointly selects parallel evaluations of one scalar objective using approximate information gain about its maximizer location, with sampled optimizer locations and Gaussian expectation-propagation approximations to conditional batch observation covariance log determinants.

definition_evidence.locator: Sections3–3.3, PDFpp.3–5, joint optimizer-information target, relaxed conditioning, EP, sampling and Eq 7.

claims.statement: Parallel predictive entropy search selects Q input locations together for parallel noisy evaluations of one scalar objective. In the source maximization convention, its ideal acquisition is I(x_star; Y_S | D), information about the global maximizer location from the joint batch observation vector. Assume a posterior over functions with a finite attained maximum on the compact search domain, a measurable maximizer selection rule when needed, and finite mutual information. Mutual information symmetry rewrites this target as joint predictive entropy minus expected joint entropy conditional on the maximizer. It remains a one-step information objective even though the batch is selected jointly.

evidence.locator: Section2, PDFp.2, problem and existence assumption; Section3, PDFp.3, Eqs1–2; Section5, PDFp.8, one-step versus within-batch distinction.

claims.statement: For a sampled maximizer location, relax the all-domain maximum condition to comparisons f(x_star) >= f(x_q) at the Q proposed locations and a soft comparison with the largest observed noisy response y_max. For positive observation noise standard deviation sigma and a nonempty observation history, the relaxed latent density is proportional to the ordinary GP posterior over batch values and f(x_star), multiplied by the Q comparison indicators and Phi((f(x_star) - y_max)/sigma). Normalize this product. The noisy incumbent factor is a heuristic restriction; it neither checks every past latent function value nor excludes a larger unqueried value, and the result is not exact global-maximizer conditioning.

evidence.locator: Section3.1, PDFpp.3–4, relaxed conditions and Eq 4; Eq 4 omits the required normalization.
PDFp.1, Eq 1 states the relaxed product with proportionality.

claims.statement: Approximate each hard comparison and the soft incumbent factor with a scaled Gaussian site along a linear projection of the Q + 1 latent values. Hard sites use f(x_star) - f(x_q), and the incumbent site uses f(x_star). EP updates projected cavity moments and site parameters. A proper resulting Gaussian supplies a full conditional covariance across all Q query locations by marginalizing out f(x_star). Add independent observation-noise covariance sigma^2 I after latent approximation. This keeps dependence among batch locations within the Gaussian approximation; it does not establish exact conditional moments or guaranteed EP convergence.

evidence.locator: Section3.1, PDFp.4, site directions, covariance part of Eq 5, Gaussian marginalization and observation-noise addition.
PDFpp.1–2, Eqs1–4 and6–14, intended EP site/cavity/moment structure; literal formula defects are retained below.

claims.statement: For a stationary kernel with a normalized spectral density, form random Fourier features with amplitude sqrt(2 alpha / m), sample linear feature weights from their Gaussian posterior and optimize the sampled feature function to approximate a posterior maximizer draw. Finite feature counts and local numerical maximization introduce approximation. The paper also describes using the maximizer of the posterior mean as a single-location plug-in; its identification of that location with the MAP of the optimizer distribution is not valid in general. The reported experiments use random features and reject draws leading to failed EP runs, a policy that can change the distribution of retained optimizer samples.

evidence.locator: Section3.2, PDFpp.4–5, posterior-mean plug-in, Eq 6 and feature posterior; Section4, PDFp.6, rejection of failed EP runs. The MAP identification is a source caveat, not adopted as an identity.

claims.statement: For each sampled hyperparameter setting and approximate maximizer, compute one half of the difference between log det(K + sigma^2 I) and log det(Sigma + sigma^2 I), where K is the ordinary latent batch covariance and Sigma is the EP conditional latent batch covariance. Average these differences over the samples as in Eq 7, with one half multiplying the whole difference. Positive-definite observation covariances are required for these finite Gaussian entropies. The Q-by-Q determinants retain batch correlation; they are generally different from a sum of single-query log-variance acquisitions and are unchanged by consistent permutation of batch indices. At Q = 1 the determinants reduce to variances. Hyperparameter averaging is an average of conditional information approximations, not generally the entropy difference of a fully marginalized predictive mixture.

evidence.locator: Section3, PDFp.3, Gaussian predictive entropy; Section3.1, PDFp.4, conditional entropy; Section3.3, PDFp.5, Eq 7 and hyperparameter sampling; Section4, PDFp.6, batch permutation symmetry.

claims.statement: Optimize the approximate acquisition jointly over the Q times input dimension coordinates rather than filling the batch by independent single-query choices. The published covariance derivative in Eq 9 holds the fitted EP site variances fixed while differentiating the GP covariance. It is valid under that fixed-site convention; convergence of EP does not generally make the site parameters independent of GP parameters, so this expression is not certified as the derivative through refitted EP or of exact mutual information. The reported random initialization followed by gradient ascent is local numerical optimization and does not guarantee the globally best batch or an optimal multi-step evaluation policy.

evidence.locator: Section3.3, PDFp.5, Eqs 8–9 and site-derivative assertion; Section4, PDFp.8, initialization and admitted local-optimization limitation; Section5, PDFp.8, one-step information objective.

entries.identity_notes: The original PPES method seeks joint information from a batch about a single-objective maximizer using sampled optimizer locations, EP and full batch predictive covariance. Scalar PES does not itself specify that joint-batch acquisition, and constrained multi-objective PPESMOC targets a different random object. Historical PPES abstract-only and future-extension mentions were research context, not a maintained record.
limitations: Compactness alone does not guarantee finite attained maxima for arbitrary sample functions. A posterior maximizer target, tie-selection convention and finite information must be well defined. The displayed noisy-incumbent factor assumes a nonempty history and positive sigma; the record does not specify a general zero-noise, singular-covariance or empty-history implementation.

Official NIPS 2015 main PDF has 9 pages; its linked ZIP contains a separate 2 page supplement. arXiv 1511.07130v1 was submitted November 23, 2015 and has 12 pages including the appendix. The checked method and appendix displays retain the same substantive caveats; publication, submission and PDF build dates are kept distinct. No author implementation was inspected or executed.

Main Eq 4 on p.4 omits normalization, while supplement Eq 1 uses proportionality. Main Eq 5 and supplement Eq 3 give a malformed Gaussian mean update with a vector-plus-matrix sum and inverse. The covariance part is the supported precision-addition form. The record does not certify a literal implementation of the printed mean formula.

Supplement p.1 Eq 5 has a site sum stopping at Q despite Q+1 sites and inconsistent parameter notation. On p.2, Eq 7 uses projected inverse covariance instead of the projected covariance in the cavity-variance calculation; Eq 11 uses squared cavity mean where the derivative identity requires squared cavity variance; beta for the soft site contains an extra Phi; Eqs10–11 omit the soft-probit noise-dependent moment factors; Eq 13 inverts a natural-mean difference that should be multiplied by the site variance. These are inspected source algebra caveats, not a claimed author erratum or complete repaired PPES implementation.

The posterior-mean maximizer is not generally the posterior mode of the maximizer location. A finite three-point Gaussian example with means (1,0,0) and variances (0.01,100,100) gives the first point a win probability below one third, despite its uniquely highest mean; symmetry gives each other point a larger optimizer probability. The supporting audit uses an analytic upper bound and a differentiable-kernel realization, not Monte Carlo estimation.

Converged EP site parameters can depend on the prior. For one standard zero-threshold Gaussian truncation with prior variance v, the projected variance is c v, c = 1 - 2/pi, and site precision is (1/c - 1)/v. The derivative through refitting is c, whereas freezing the site gives c^2. This bounded counterexample refutes general site constancy; it does not implement the complete PPES acquisition or audit all hypotheses of its cited EP references.

Finite random features, approximate maximizer search, relaxed conditioning, Gaussian EP projection, rejected failed EP samples, Monte Carlo hyperparameters and local batch optimization all affect the operational approximation. The Figure 1 reference calculation itself uses discretization, rejection sampling and a kernel-density entropy estimate. The p.7 experimental prose says 200 random initializations while the Figure 3 caption on p.8 says 100; no aggregate empirical count or performance conclusion is adopted. No exact noisy information, unbiased accepted-sample, global-optimization, universal accuracy, runtime or superiority claim is made.

The original bounded checks in research/discovery/ppes-boundaries.py use rational matrices and finite information channels, plus explicitly floating Gaussian CDF, moment and entropy calculations. They are supporting algebra and counterexamples, not full EP inference, external-code execution, a GP benchmark or independent scientific approval. Scalar PES, scalar optimum-value MES/OPES and constrained multi-objective PPESMOC remain distinct operational identities; the Q = 1 ideal-information overlap does not identify their approximations.

This relates to querying an information source, but scalar black-box optimization is not identical to the pinned task of labeling data for predictive learning. entries.name: DIRECT global optimization
entries.definition: A deterministic derivative-free global optimization algorithm that adaptively partitions a bounded real search box, samples rectangle centers and trisects the longest sides of every rectangle that is potentially optimal for some positive rate-of-change weight and a specified score-improvement threshold.

definition_evidence.locator: Sections 3–4, PDF pp.7–16 / printed pp.163–172, especially Definitions 3.1 and4.1 and the rectangle division procedure.

claims.statement: For minimization of a finite-valued deterministic scalar objective on a finite-dimensional box with strictly positive side lengths, normalize each coordinate to [0,1]. Start with the unit hypercube and evaluate its center. Maintain a partition into axis-aligned hyperrectangles, each with an evaluated center, and retain the smallest objective value observed. The defining search uses function values rather than objective derivatives or a fitted probabilistic surrogate. The geometry is measured in normalized coordinates, so the original coordinate bounds affect its metric.

evidence.locator: Sections 3–4, PDF pp.7–14 / printed pp.163–170; center sampling, normalization and multivariate algorithm Step 1.

claims.statement: Let c_i be each rectangle center and d_i its Euclidean distance to a vertex, equal to one half of its diagonal length in normalized coordinates. For a fixed epsilon > 0 and current best value f_min, rectangle j is potentially optimal when some finite K_tilde > 0 satisfies both f(c_j) - K_tilde d_j <= f(c_i) - K_tilde d_i for every current rectangle i, and f(c_j) - K_tilde d_j <= f_min - epsilon |f_min|. All such rectangles are eligible, including distinct rectangles tied at the same distance and value. The rate-of-change weight is varied rather than supplied as a known Lipschitz bound; its score is not automatically a certified lower bound on the objective inside the rectangle.

evidence.locator: Definition 3.1, PDF p.9 / printed p.165, and Definition 4.1, PDF p.14 / printed p.170; distinction from a known Lipschitz constant on PDF p.10 / printed p.166.

claims.statement: For each selected rectangle, collect all dimensions whose side length equals its maximum side length L. Evaluate the objective at c plus and minus (L/3)e_i for every such dimension i. Order these dimensions by the smaller of their two sampled values. Trisect the rectangle containing the original center along the best dimension, then continue splitting only the remaining central rectangle along each subsequent dimension. With m tied longest dimensions, this creates 2m + 1 child rectangles from 2m new center samples while reusing the original center value. A stated deterministic rule is needed to order dimensions with equal pair scores; different valid tie orders can produce different labeled partitions.

evidence.locator: Section 4, PDF pp.11–13 / printed pp.167–169, Figure 7 and Procedure for Dividing Rectangles, Steps 1–3; child-count and tie consequences of that procedure.

claims.statement: Determine the full potentially optimal set at the start of an iteration. Subdivide every member of that fixed set, updating the partition and the observed best value, before computing a new potentially optimal set. The original procedure processes all selected rectangles and does not replace this step by repeatedly selecting only the current best rectangle. Complete-iteration results do not depend on the order of processing disjoint selected rectangles when within-rectangle tie conventions are fixed and evaluations are deterministic. An iteration can contain multiple new evaluations. The source uses a specified iteration limit and also permits an evaluation budget; an early budget stop may interrupt the complete-iteration convention.

evidence.locator: Univariate algorithm Steps 2–7 and order discussion, PDF pp.10–11 / printed pp.166–167; multivariate algorithm Steps 2–6, PDF pp.14–16 / printed pp.170–172.

claims.statement: Epsilon imposes a required improvement on the weighted selection score relative to |f_min|; it is not a verified error bound or stopping tolerance. At f_min = 0 the epsilon term vanishes, although the remaining selection inequalities still apply. Multiplying all objective values by a positive constant preserves the exact selection test after rescaling K_tilde. Adding a constant generally does not, because |f_min| changes. For example, with epsilon = 1/100, a best small interval of radius 1/18 and value 0 competes with larger intervals of radius 1/6 and value 1 for 0 < K_tilde <= 9. Adding 100 to every value requires K_tilde >= 18 for the small interval, so it ceases to be potentially optimal despite unchanged objective rankings.

evidence.locator: Definitions 3.1 and 4.1, PDF pp.9 and14 / printed pp.165 and170; epsilon discussion, PDF pp.10 and23 / printed pp.166 and179. Scaling and translation statements are direct algebraic consequences, checked in the supporting exact calculator.

claims.statement: For the ideal original algorithm continued indefinitely with exact selection, complete iterations and finite objective values, at least one rectangle with maximal center-to-vertex distance is selected each iteration. Repeated longest-side trisection makes the maximum rectangle radius tend to zero, so sampled centers become dense in the box. If a finite global minimum is attained and the objective is continuous in a neighborhood of a global minimizer, the best sampled values converge to that minimum. This is an asymptotic value statement, not a finite-budget error certificate, a rate guarantee, exact finite attainment of a boundary minimizer or a guarantee for arbitrary discontinuous objectives and modified selection rules.

evidence.locator: Section 5, PDF pp.17–18 / printed pp.173–174, Eq 9 and dense-sampling argument; stopping limitation on PDF p.3 / printed p.159. The zero-denominator caveat in printed Eq 11 is retained below.

entries.identity_notes: DIRECT denotes the original deterministic box-partition method: normalized-domain center sampling, potentially optimal rectangles under an unspecified positive slope, and longest-side trisection. It does not require a surrogate or an information acquisition. This differs from random or grid search, population-based differential evolution/CMA-ES, and GP-guided optimization. Direct Preference Optimization is a policy objective and is unrelated.
limitations: This record describes the original 1993 DIRECT construction. Later locally biased, tie-reduced, restart, noisy-objective, constrained or parallel variants are not silently imported or declared exact aliases. A direct-search optimizer is not the maintained DirectPreferenceOptimization algorithm.

The source uses finite-valued deterministic objective evaluations on a finite box. General constraints, failed evaluations, noise handling, categorical parameters, zero-width coordinates and floating-point degeneracy need additional implementation rules. Normalization and tie conventions can affect the search trajectory; no rotation invariance or coordinate-independent behavior is asserted.

The lower-right convex-hull interpretation concerns existence of a positive weight satisfying both inequalities. A point touching only at weight zero is excluded by the stated definition, and the epsilon filter can exclude a hull candidate. Equal-distance candidates require direct value comparison rather than division by a zero distance difference.

In the introductory Shubert comparison, PDF p.4 / printed p.160 Eq 5 omits the factor one half on K(b-a) for the claimed bottom-of-V value. With equal endpoint values 0, interval [0,2] and K=1, the intersecting lines have minimum -1, while the printed expression gives -2. That expression is a weaker lower bound in this example, not the stated intersection value. DIRECT’s center-based Eq 8 and potentially optimal definitions are separate.

The convergence proof’s Eq 11, PDF p.17 / printed p.173, writes an unrestricted maximum of ratios with denominator d_j-d_i, including equal-distance cases and i=j. The argument requires taking those ratios only over strictly smaller distances, while handling equal-distance centers by selecting a minimum-value one. This is an explicit curator reading of the definition-level proof, not an asserted author-issued correction.

Dense sampling alone does not guarantee convergence of values for arbitrary discontinuities: a function equal to -1 only at sqrt(2)/2 and 0 elsewhere on [0,1] has an isolated minimum that the exact rational center sequence never samples. Even for a continuous objective, a finite set of sampled values can miss a narrow negative tent between samples. Without additional certified function bounds, a budget stop cannot certify global accuracy.

The source’s benchmark comparisons use different convergence definitions for competing methods and discuss parameter-tuning and stochastic-run comparability problems. No benchmark was reproduced and no universal speed, dimension-independent storage, parameter-insensitivity or superiority claim is made. The central sample avoids enumerating all box vertices, but subdivision, retained rectangles and coordinate bookkeeping still require resources.

The original bounded calculator in research/discovery/direct-boundaries.py uses rational radius clouds for selection, exact multivariate partition geometry and finite one-dimensional examples. It does not implement general multivariate square-root radius selection or establish asymptotic results by testing. Its trace evaluation counts denote distinct sampled locations, not runtime function-call costs; center values may be recomputed for geometric checks. It is supporting evidence within the author workflow, not independent scientific approval or external author-code execution.

evidence_sources.title: Lipschitzian Optimization Without the Lipschitz Constant
evidence_sources.version: Original October 1993 article, JOTA 79(1):157–181; inspected 25-page academic-hosted scan. Publisher metadata corroborates bibliographic identity, not PDF byte equivalence. Scan build dates 2004/2014 are not publication dates.

aio_no_match.search_scope: Freshly assessed all 721 native and 442 pinned AIO records (1,163 total): IDs, names, aliases, scoped synonyms and complete definitions. Four whole-checkout searches used rg --no-ignore --hidden with exact IDs/full names and meaningful compounds; all 4,196 occurrences were reconciled and all 88 decoded matching contexts read. Bare DIRECT was not treated as an exhaustive identity probe; ordinary direct-algorithm phrases were false positives. All 902 main and 393 nested frontier labels/statuses, all matching fields and 29 relevant full objects were read. Nine exact examined AIO CLASS nodes (ActiveLearning, MachineLearningTask, TrainingStrategy, ReinforcementLearning, EvolutionaryLLM, MathematicalFunction, Model, Network and MarkovChain), including metadata/synonyms and every incident edge, support no suitable mapping for this deterministic rectangle-partition optimizer. TransferLearning was also inspected for the cohort. This is a scoped pinned-snapshot no-match assessment, not absence from all ontologies.
aio_no_match.rationale: No inspected pinned AIO target provides a sufficiently specific mapping for the general DIRECT optimizer. Its machine-learning uses do not make it a learning task, training preprocessing, network or model. This is an explicit bounded no-match assessment, not a claim that no suitable concept exists in another ontology.

examined_targets.rejection_reason: The general deterministic optimizer does not require labeling examples or selecting queries by learned predictive uncertainty; objective evaluation alone does not establish this learning-task mapping.
The algorithm can optimize an arbitrary box-constrained objective without building a method that learns from data; an AI application does not identify its full scope with this task.
The pinned definition concerns preprocessing and model training. DIRECT is a reusable optimizer; its use inside hyperparameter selection is an application rather than a necessary training mechanism.
Balancing local and global exploration does not make the general search procedure a policy/environment learning task.
This target is a large language model and its broad related synonyms do not denote the deterministic rectangle algorithm.
The objective and selection score are mathematical functions, but the proposed concept is the iterative partitioning algorithm, not a function node.
A partition and stored evaluations do not make this search algorithm identical to the pinned abstract model class.
The optional search-tree representation is bookkeeping, not a defining network architecture.
A generic state representation would be too broad; DIRECT does not define a stochastic transition process or target-invariant sampler.

entries.name: Expected improvement acquisition
entries.definition: An acquisition criterion for deterministic scalar minimization that scores a candidate evaluation by the predictive expected positive reduction below the best observed objective value, with a closed form in the predictive mean and standard deviation under Gaussian uncertainty.

definition_evidence.locator: Section 4.1, PDF pp.17–18 / printed pp.471–472, Eqs.14–15 and deterministic-uncertainty interpretation.

claims.statement: For deterministic scalar minimization, let b be the smallest observed objective value and Y the predictive uncertainty about the value at a candidate input. Expected improvement is E[max(b - Y, 0)]. It weights each positive improvement by its predictive probability, retaining the amount of gain rather than only the probability P(Y < b). The random variable represents uncertainty about an unevaluated deterministic function, not observation noise.

evidence.locator: Section 4.1, PDF p.17 / printed p.471, improvement definition and Eq.14.

claims.statement: If Y is Gaussian with mean m and strictly positive standard deviation s, define z = (b - m)/s. Then EI = (b - m) Phi(z) + s phi(z), where Phi and phi are the standard normal distribution and density. The denominator and density multiplier use s, not the variance s squared. In the inspected EGO construction, m and s come from a fitted DACE predictor and its estimated prediction error.

evidence.locator: Section 4.1, PDF pp.17–18 / printed pp.471–472, Eq.15 and definitions of Y, s, Phi and phi.

claims.statement: Holding the incumbent fixed with finite m and s > 0, the partial derivatives are dEI/dm = -Phi(z) and dEI/ds = phi(z). EI therefore decreases with predictive mean and increases with predictive standard deviation when the other argument is fixed. A lower bound on m and an upper bound on s give an EI upper bound over an input box. These are partial derivatives of the score, not assertions of monotonicity in the input coordinates.

evidence.locator: Section 4.1, PDF pp.18–19 / printed pp.472–473, displayed partial derivatives and rectangular-region bound.

claims.statement: For a degenerate predictive law with s = 0, Eq.14 gives EI = max(b - m, 0); division by s in Eq.15 is not defined there. Under exact noiseless interpolation at an already observed input, m equals its observed value and is at least b, so EI is zero. Zero variance by itself does not imply zero improvement at an arbitrary input. The general degenerate-law statement is a direct curator derivation from the defining expectation.

evidence.locator: Section 2, PDF pp.7–9 / printed pp.461–463, Eqs.7–11 and interpolation; Section 4.1, PDF pp.17–18 / printed pp.471–472, Eq.14 and zero-at-samples statement; general s = 0 qualification follows from Eq.14.

claims.statement: EI assesses the gain from one prospective evaluation relative to the current incumbent. Its maximization supplies a query-selection rule, but the score alone does not specify a surrogate-fitting procedure, initial design, stopping policy or complete sequential optimizer. The original EGO algorithm combines this criterion with those additional stages; EI is not an exact alias for EGO.

evidence.locator: Section 4.1, PDF pp.17–19 / printed pp.471–473; Section 4.2, PDF pp.19–21 / printed pp.473–475, algorithm and one-additional-point limitation.

entries.identity_notes: Expected improvement is the expected nonnegative gain relative to a stated threshold; it is a criterion rather than a full optimizer. TPE implements a particular density-model ranking and SMAC uses expected-improvement proposals inside a broader configuration procedure. Neither maintained record is the general EI criterion. Probability of improvement measures an event probability rather than gain magnitude; EGO uses EI within a complete original optimization procedure.
limitations: The inspected formulation uses noiseless observations and a fixed observed incumbent. With noisy data, the best observation need not be the best latent value, and expected improvement in a noisy measurement is not generally improvement in the underlying objective. Uncertainty in a latent incumbent would require an appropriate joint model. Section 6, PDF p.33 / printed p.487 explicitly leaves noisy-function optimization unresolved; no noisy, constrained, batch or multiobjective EI extension is specified here.

The DACE mean and prediction error use estimated correlation and variance parameters. Their uncertainty is not fully integrated, and the source notes that its standard error may be too small. Expected gain is conditional on that predictive approximation; it is neither a calibrated probability-of-success guarantee nor a bound on the true remaining optimization error (Section 2, PDF p.9 / printed p.463; Section 4.2, PDF pp.20–21 / printed pp.474–475).

Changing the objective by a nonlinear increasing transformation preserves its ordering but can change improvement magnitudes and acquisition rankings. The source actually fits transformed responses in EGO. EI on the transformed scale must not be identified with EI on the original scale or obtained by applying the transform to a predicted mean alone. The transformation distinction is supported by the inspected procedure and separate bounded curator examples, not by a universal invariance claim (Section 4.2, PDF pp.19–20 / printed pp.473–474).

EI depends on both predictive location and spread. It is distinct from probability of improvement, variance maximization and optimizer-information acquisitions. The original bounded curator checks separate exact rational interpolation from floating Gaussian CDF, quadrature, derivative and transformation examples; they do not implement EGO or establish numerical accuracy in extreme Gaussian tails.

Evidence is the 38-page journal-layout mirror of Jones, Schonlau and Welch (1998), not a verified byte-identical publisher download. The separate 43-page author manuscript was cover-inspected only, and the cited Mockus et al. (1978) chapter was not obtained. No earliest-invention claim is made. The source Appendix 1 derivative-sign discrepancy and fixed-correlation Hessian caveat concern separate surrogate derivations and do not change the defining EI expectation or its positive-standard-deviation formula.

entries.name: Efficient Global Optimization
entries.definition: The original sequential optimization algorithm of Jones, Schonlau and Welch for expensive deterministic scalar functions on bounded continuous boxes, combining a space-filling initial design, fitted and diagnostically assessed DACE response models, expected-improvement acquisition search, objective evaluation and model refitting.

definition_evidence.locator: Section 4.2, PDF pp.19–22 / printed pp.473–476, original EGO procedure; Sections 2–4.1, PDF pp.4–19 / printed pp.458–473, surrogate, diagnostics and EI dependencies.

claims.statement: The original EGO procedure begins with evaluations of an expensive deterministic scalar objective on a bounded rectangular search region using a space-filling Latin-hypercube design. The described design search aims at nearly uniform one- and two-dimensional projections. These initial evaluations supply the data for the first DACE fit; the suggested initial sample size is a heuristic, not a defining fixed count or convergence condition.

evidence.locator: Section 4.2, PDF p.19 / printed p.473, initial design and empirical sample-size discussion; PDF p.22 / printed p.476, bounded-box setting.

claims.statement: Fit a constant-mean DACE response model with a product-exponential distance correlation, exp(-sum_h theta_h |x_h - x_prime_h|^p_h). Maximum likelihood estimates its parameters. The predictor uses the correlation matrix R and candidate correlation vector r; its prediction-error expression includes the constant-mean estimation term. The ordinary-inverse formulas require nonsingular R. Estimated correlation and process-variance parameters are plugged in rather than fully integrated out.

evidence.locator: Section 2, PDF pp.5–9 / printed pp.459–463, Eqs.1–9 and estimated-parameter qualification; Section 4.2, PDF pp.19–20 / printed pp.473–474, maximum-likelihood fitting.

claims.statement: Inspect cross-validated predictions and standardized residuals before the sequential search. In the stated practical leave-one-out procedure, covariance parameters fitted to the full sample are retained. If diagnostics are unsatisfactory, refit after a suitable response transformation, such as the displayed log or reciprocal transformations on their applicable domains. Continue on the chosen response scale only if diagnostics are satisfactory; the source would abandon the method if no satisfactory transformation were found.

evidence.locator: Section 3, PDF pp.12–15 / printed pp.466–469, practical cross-validation and transformations; Section 4.2, PDF pp.19–20 / printed pp.473–474, diagnostic decision and response-scale choices.

claims.statement: Choose an evaluation location by maximizing Gaussian expected improvement below the best observed value on the modeled response scale. The full acquisition search uses rectangular branch and bound: a lower bound on predictive mean and an upper bound on predictive standard deviation provide an EI upper bound. The paper derives surrogate bounds through relaxations of the correlation constraints. Its implemented strong predictor-bound construction and reported examples use p_h = 2; this does not establish a ready implementation for every correlation exponent.

evidence.locator: Section 4.1, PDF pp.17–19 / printed pp.471–473, Eq.15 and bound; Section 4.2, PDF p.20 / printed p.474, implemented p_h = 2 scope; Sections 4.3–4.4, PDF pp.22–26 / printed pp.476–480, bound constructions.

claims.statement: Evaluate the objective at the selected location, augment the data and re-estimate the DACE parameters by maximum likelihood before the next acquisition. A tolerance on maximum expected improvement controls stopping. The reported relative-change rule and its log-scale approximation are heuristics: one-step expected gain under a fitted surrogate is not a certificate of the true error or the total gain available from all further evaluations.

evidence.locator: Section 4.2, PDF pp.19–21 / printed pp.473–475, sampling/refitting loop, stopping rule, log-scale approximation and stated limitations.

claims.statement: The reported six-dimensional Hartman run does not use the full acquisition search to convergence. It retains only the best 50 branch-and-bound nodes, caps that search at 500 iterations, then refines the result by local search. The source explicitly recognizes that this limited-memory variant can miss the true EI maximum. Its behavior must be distinguished from the full bounding procedure; the stated numerical limits are experimental settings, not a definition of every EGO run.

evidence.locator: Section 4.2, PDF p.21 / printed p.475, limited-memory branch and bound and admitted acquisition-maximization risk.

entries.identity_notes: EGO is the original sequential procedure for expensive deterministic objectives, combining a design, Kriging model fitting, expected-improvement maximization and stopping. It is not just the EI functional. Existing SMAC uses a random-forest configuration model and instance intensification; ES/PES use optimizer-information acquisitions. Efficient Global Optimization in later paper titles does not establish identity with the original Jones procedure.
limitations: This identity denotes the original deterministic scalar procedure, not every Bayesian optimizer or every method using EI. No noisy-objective, nonlinear-constraint, derivative-enabled, multifidelity, batch or multiobjective extension is absorbed. Section 6, PDF p.33 / printed p.487 discusses such extensions separately and leaves noisy-function EGO unresolved. EI itself is a distinct acquisition rule; TPE and SMAC use different model and search machinery.

The source does not prove global convergence. Conjecture 1 assumes correlation parameters theta_h bounded away from zero, a continuous objective on a finite box and an indefinitely continued search; it remains explicitly unproved (Section 4.2, PDF p.22 / printed p.476). Acquisition bounds, empirical examples and a model-based stopping threshold do not establish finite-budget optimality or universal performance.

Nonlinear response transformations can change improvement magnitudes and query rankings. The literal 1% stopping rule needs a sign and scale convention when the incumbent is zero or negative; no absolute-value replacement or numerical floor is silently supplied. The log-scale tolerance is described as an approximate relative change. Plug-in uncertainty and one-step gain also limit interpretation of that stopping rule (Section 4.2, PDF pp.19–21 / printed pp.473–475).

Very smooth responses and closely spaced inputs can make R nearly singular. The authors report singular-value decomposition with small singular values set to zero, but the record does not certify a particular truncation threshold, ordinary-inverse validity after truncation, or preservation of all interpolation and bounding properties (Section 6, PDF p.32 / printed p.486).

Appendix 1, PDF p.36 / printed p.490, changes the negative cross term of the displayed quadratic into a positive term in its derivative. Differentiation requires a minus sign to recover the stated predictor Eq.7. The inspected discrepancy and separate exact sign witness are retained as source algebra context, not an asserted author erratum or a repaired EGO implementation.

For fixed real symmetric positive-definite R, fixed nonnegative process variance and exact arithmetic, the Eq.16 Hessian is positive semidefinite with a zero eigenvalue, so the Eq.17 alpha correction is zero. The separate curator derivation uses A = R_inverse - (R_inverse 1)(R_inverse 1)^T/(1^T R_inverse 1). This qualifies the source discussion of a possible negative eigenvalue. Nonlinear constraints linking r and x remain nonconvex; neither EI concavity, convexity of the full search problem nor a numerical failure in the authors’ implementation follows (Section 4.3, PDF pp.22–24 / printed pp.476–478; Appendix 2, PDF p.36 / printed p.490).

Primary method evidence is the 38-page journal-layout mirror of the 1998 paper. The distinct 43-page author manuscript was cover-inspected only; exact equivalence to that manuscript or an inaccessible publisher download was not established. The cited Mockus et al. (1978) chapter was not read, so no earliest-invention claim is made.

The supporting original calculations and separate root reproductions check bounded EI, interpolation and source-sign examples. Exact rational checks are distinct from floating Gaussian, quadrature and transformation calculations. The separate Hessian assessment is an analytic derivation under stated assumptions. None executes author code, implements the complete EGO search, replicates its benchmarks or supplies a formal erratum or convergence proof.

aio_mappings.rationale: Original EGO adaptively queries an objective and updates a data-derived response model, relating it to the pinned concept of querying an information source for outputs. Deterministic black-box optimization is not identical to a data-labeling task, and this qualified association imposes neither an annotation requirement nor an upstream subclass or exact-match assertion.

entries.name: Probability of improvement acquisition
entries.definition: An acquisition criterion for scalar optimization that scores a candidate by the predictive probability of meeting a specified improvement threshold under a stated direction and tie convention, with a Gaussian cumulative-distribution form when the predictive law is Gaussian and its standard deviation is positive.

definition_evidence.locator: Section 6, PDF p.20 / printed p.364, improvement-threshold event and Eq.27.
Section 2.2, PDF p.3, probability-of-improvement definition and Eq.1.

claims.statement: Probability of improvement scores a candidate by the predictive probability of meeting a specified improvement threshold. For minimization, Jones defines the event Y(x) <= T with T below the best observed value; Snoek and colleagues use improvement over the current-best value. The predictive random variable expresses uncertainty about the candidate value. The direction, threshold and strict or inclusive event convention must be stated; the criterion does not itself prescribe a unique target schedule.

evidence.locator: Section 6, PDF p.20 / printed p.364, definition of Y(x), T < f_min and the event Y(x) <= T preceding Eq.27.
Section 2.2, PDF p.3, incumbent notation and probability-of-improvement definition preceding Eq.1.

claims.statement: For a Gaussian predictive value with mean m and strictly positive standard deviation s, the minimization score at threshold T is Phi((T - m)/s), where Phi is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. For maximization the corresponding event has score Phi((m - T)/s). The maximization expression follows by reversing the event direction. The denominator is the standard deviation, not the variance. Strict and inclusive events have the same probability in this positive-variance Gaussian case.

evidence.locator: Section 6, PDF p.20 / printed p.364, Eq.27 and standard-error definition; maximization and continuity qualifications are direct event derivations.
Section 2.2, PDF p.3, Eq.1 and predictive variance notation sigma squared.

claims.statement: PI measures the probability of its threshold event rather than the magnitude of gain beyond the threshold. Expected improvement instead averages a nonnegative improvement amount. Consequently the two criteria can rank candidates differently even under Gaussian predictions and the same incumbent. This distinction concerns their objectives and does not assert a universal performance ordering between them.

evidence.locator: Section 2.2, PDF p.3, separate PI and EI definitions in Eqs.1–2; possible ranking difference follows directly from the two formulas.
Section 6, PDF p.20 / printed p.364, Eq.27; Section 7, PDF p.27 / printed p.371, Eqs.34–35.

claims.statement: At zero predictive variance the random value equals m, so the minimization probability is the indicator of m < T for a strict event or m <= T for an inclusive event. In particular, at m = T these probabilities are zero and one, respectively. For every positive Gaussian standard deviation at m = T, the CDF score is one half, even as s tends to zero. The singular point-mass case therefore requires the declared event convention instead of division by zero or an unconditional zero rule. These boundary statements are direct curator derivations from the event definition.

evidence.locator: Section 6, PDF p.20 / printed p.364, inclusive event preceding Eq.27; the point-mass extension is derived from that event, not a printed source algorithm.
Section 2.2, PDF p.3, Eq.1; its positive-standard-deviation expression supplies the tie-limit comparison.

claims.statement: Snoek and colleagues explicitly integrate PI over the posterior distribution of Gaussian-process hyperparameters. When the same threshold event is used for every hyperparameter setting, the average conditional probability is the probability under the predictive mixture, by the law of total probability. This does not require replacing the mixture by a Gaussian. Evaluating a Gaussian CDF using only the mixture mean and variance is generally a different approximation. The latter distinction is a curator qualification of the stated integration rule.

evidence.locator: Section 3.1, PDF p.4, Eq.6 and the following paragraph explicitly naming probability of improvement and EI; fixed-event and moment-matching qualifications follow from the probability definition.

claims.statement: Maximizing PI can supply a next-evaluation rule, but the scalar criterion alone does not specify an initial design, predictive model fitting, numerical acquisition optimizer, stopping rule or complete sequential search procedure. Jones combines the criterion with additional steps in Method 4 and describes a separate enhanced procedure with multiple targets. Those procedures are not exact aliases for the criterion, and their empirical behavior or convergence properties are not inherited by its definition.

evidence.locator: Section 2, PDF p.2, separate model and acquisition choices; Section 2.2, PDF p.3, next-query maximization and PI Eq.1.
Section 6, PDF pp.20–26 / printed pp.364–370, Method 4, target selection and Enhanced Method 4.

entries.identity_notes: PI is the predictive probability of meeting a stated improvement threshold, with an explicit strict or inclusive event convention. Its positive-variance Gaussian CDF form is a model-specific evaluation of that event, not the general definition of an optimizer. It differs from EI's expected gain and from MES's information target; a bounded one-sample ranking relation does not make PI and MES identical. The maintained PiModel is a semi-supervised consistency method and is unrelated.
limitations: For a minimization incumbent b and margin xi >= 0, setting T = b - xi gives gain > xi for a strict event and gain >= xi for an inclusive event. Positive-variance Gaussian continuity makes their probabilities equal, but this equality does not extend to arbitrary predictive atoms. The zero-variance event must be evaluated directly; the printed formulas do not specify every degenerate convention.

Snoek Section 2.2, PDF p.3 observes noisy y_n but expresses the incumbent through latent f(x_n). The inspected passage does not prescribe a unique operational noisy-incumbent estimator. A fixed data-derived threshold, an uncertain latent incumbent and a future noisy measurement define different events. A random incumbent requires its joint dependence with the prospective value; substituting its mean is not generally equivalent. No particular noisy, batch, constrained or multiobjective extension is specified here.

The target policy is intentionally not reconstructed from the examples. Jones PDF p.21 / printed p.365 uses an observed-best target, whereas the captions on PDF pp.22–23 / printed pp.366–367 describe percentages below the surface minimum; Enhanced Method 4 separately uses a surface-minimum and observed-range formula on PDF p.23. The p.21 wording about T being too high and global search also conflicts with the decreasing-target direction on p.23. These distinctions are retained as source ambiguities, not silently unified into one schedule or presented as formal errata.

A high PI value is conditional on the chosen predictive model and event; it is not a calibrated guarantee about the unknown objective or the remaining optimization error. Increasing predictive spread does not universally increase PI: for a fixed minimization threshold its direction depends on the mean relative to that threshold. The retained bounded examples separate probability and gain rankings without establishing a universal advantage for either acquisition.

Hyperparameter integration in Snoek PDF p.4 concerns averaging conditional acquisition values. For a fixed event, probability averaging is valid; replacing the predictive mixture by a Gaussian using its first two moments generally changes the score. If the threshold varies with hyperparameters or represents a random incumbent, the joint event must be specified rather than identified with the same fixed-threshold probability.

Jones PDF pp.25–26 / printed pp.369–370 derives a matching lower-confidence-bound coefficient from an attained ratio optimum with positive standard errors. That coefficient depends on the target and current predictive functions and need not be nonnegative. A fixed target is therefore not a fixed confidence-bound policy. Snoek PDF p.3 also gives an unnegated lower-confidence expression alongside a generic acquisition-maximization convention; that ancillary direction convention does not change PI Eq.1. Restricted ranking correspondences do not make PI identical to confidence-bound or entropy-information acquisitions.

Evidence is the typeset 2001 Jones article on a university mirror and the official nine-page 2012 Snoek proceedings PDF. Publication, PDF build and acquisition metadata are distinct. The cited Kushner (1964) original PDF was not obtained after a publisher HTTP403 response, and no historical-priority or original-algorithm reconstruction claim is made. Cited convergence results and complete empirical procedures were not reproduced or adopted.

The separate original curator calculations use exact Fraction arithmetic for finite events and ratio algebra, and floating Gaussian and entropy functions for bounded examples. They are not author-code replication, a fitted Gaussian-process optimizer, a benchmark, a general convergence proof or validation of extreme-tail numerical accuracy.
