entries.name: Multi-task Bayesian optimization
entries.definition: The original Swersky–Snoek–Adams 2013 family of Bayesian optimization procedures that uses a Gaussian process with separable finite-task and configuration covariance to transfer evaluation information across related tasks, with distinct target-only transfer, average-task expected-improvement and cost-sensitive primary-task entropy-search configurations.

definition_evidence.locator: Sections 2.2–3.3, PDF pp. 2–5, task covariance and three query configurations; Section 5, PDF p. 8, original family scope.

claims.statement: Represent related objective functions over a common configuration domain as finitely indexed tasks of a Gaussian process. The separable pair covariance is B[t,t_prime]*kx(x,x_prime), where B is a task covariance matrix and kx is an input covariance. The source uses a Matern 5/2 input kernel and samples covariance parameters by slice sampling. It parameterizes B through a Cholesky factor with positive free entries to favor positive task correlations. This is a restricted task-covariance fit, not an arbitrary signed task relation or necessarily a unit-diagonal correlation matrix. A literal full Kronecker observed Gram matrix requires a complete Cartesian task/input design; general observed pairs use the corresponding covariance entries.

evidence.locator: Sections 2.1–2.2, PDF pp. 2–3, Equation 3 and covariance-parameter sampling description; Figure 1 on p. 4 is a broader illustrative task process.

claims.statement: In the transfer configuration, condition the multi-task surrogate on observations from previous related-task optimizations and on the target task. Restrict future evaluations to the target task and continue its Bayesian optimization, illustrated with expected improvement. Learning a useful task relationship requires target observations; previous tasks supply surrogate information rather than a rule that copies their best configuration as the target optimum. This configuration does not dynamically select cheaper auxiliary tasks for future evaluation.

evidence.locator: Section 3.1, PDF p. 3; Figure 1, PDF p. 4; Section 2.3, PDF p. 3, Equations 4–5; Section 4.1, PDF p. 6, direct-transfer comparator.

claims.statement: A separate configuration minimizes the average objective over k tasks. Its predictive mean is the average of task means and its variance is the sum of every posterior task-pair covariance divided by k squared. The proposed two-step heuristic imputes missing observations using predictive means, chooses a configuration by expected improvement for the estimated average function, and then selects the task with highest single-task expected improvement at that configuration. It spends one task evaluation per selected query. This is an average-task objective and an explicit heuristic, not the cost-sensitive primary-task entropy policy.

evidence.locator: Section 3.2, PDF p. 4, Equation 8 and the two-step heuristic; Section 4.2, PDF pp. 6–7, cross-validation interpretation.

claims.statement: For the entropy configuration, represent the primary task minimum by a distribution over a finite candidate set. In the usual no-tie Gaussian setting, the event that a candidate minimizes the represented function is the conjunction of comparisons with all other represented values. The ideal one-step score is the expected reduction in entropy of that primary-task minimizer after a prospective noisy observation, including an observation of a correlated auxiliary task. Its target is not the auxiliary task minimizer or the identity of the best task. The source describes Monte Carlo approximation to this information calculation; finite representation and sampling do not make the continuous-domain minimizer law exact.

evidence.locator: Section 2.3, PDF p. 3, Equations 6–7 and Monte Carlo discussion; Section 3.3, PDF pp. 4–5, primary-task target.

claims.statement: The dynamic configuration compares configuration/task queries by approximate expected reduction of primary-task minimizer entropy per positive evaluation cost. Equation 9 divides by c_t(x); the source models log evaluation cost with multi-task Gaussian-process machinery when costs are unknown. It computes this acquisition on a finite candidate subset selected by high expected improvement on the primary task, then obtains evaluations from the selected task as the optimization proceeds. Task relationships and costs can be learned during the search. The inspected description does not uniquely specify how posterior uncertainty in cost is integrated into the denominator.

evidence.locator: Section 3.3, PDF p. 5, Equation 9, log-cost model and fixed candidate subset; Section 4.3, PDF p. 7, dynamic estimation of tasks, correlation and costs.

claims.statement: The original method family shares a task-correlated surrogate but distinguishes target-only transfer, average-task optimization and dynamic cost-sensitive primary-task optimization. These policies need not choose the same inputs or tasks and do not all use an entropy acquisition or cost normalization. Tasks share a configuration domain in the described model; extending the framework across different model architectures is listed as future work rather than supplied as a general construction.

evidence.locator: Section 1, PDF p. 2; Sections 3.1–3.3, PDF pp. 3–5; Section 5, PDF p. 8, summary of configurations and multiple-architecture future work.

entries.identity_notes: This record scopes the original 2013 finite-task multi-task Bayesian optimization construction and its three differentiated policies: target-only transfer, average-task two-step expected-improvement selection, and dynamic primary-minimizer information per positive cost. It is not generic multi-task learning. FABOLAS instead models a continuous dataset-size input with special covariance and cost structure; PESC/PESC-F resource scheduling concerns objective/constraint tasks and acquisition-update costs, not this task-transfer identity.
limitations: This identity is scoped to the original 2013 finite-task family, not every later method called multi-task Bayesian optimization. It is neither the multi-task GP model alone nor a synonym for one acquisition formula. FABOLAS uses a continuous dataset-size coordinate and size-specific surrogate assumptions; PESC and its scheduling variants target constrained optimization with different inference and task semantics. Shared information-per-cost language does not establish identity.

The positive free-Cholesky fit in Section 2.2, PDF p. 2, restricts the representable task covariances. The anticorrelated process in Figure 1 on p. 4 illustrates a broader multi-task GP and does not establish arbitrary signed correlation support for that fit. Kernel fit and task similarity can be inadequate; no guaranteed beneficial transfer follows.

Section 3.3, PDF p. 5, states that a realized entropy decrease is positive and that an auxiliary query at the same input can never be more informative than a primary query. Neither is a general consequence of the stated noisy model. Coherent expected entropy reduction is nonnegative, but individual posterior entropies can increase. A fixed-hyperparameter two-input Gaussian construction with input correlation 1/2, task covariance [[1,2],[2,5]] and observation-noise variance 1 makes the rescaled auxiliary a less noisy channel for a nonconstant primary-minimizer event than the direct primary query. This bounded analytic counterexample qualifies the prose; it is not a general dominance claim, numerical experiment or author-issued erratum.

The perfect-correlation redundancy example after Equation 8, PDF p. 4, needs an observation qualification: independently noisy evaluations can remain informative even for perfectly correlated latent tasks. The average-task variance includes cross-task covariances and must not be replaced by a sum of marginal variances alone.

Positive cost division and modeling log cost do not choose a unique posterior cost convention. Expected information divided by expected cost, expected information per random cost, and division by an exponentiated mean log cost are generally different. No later implementation or paper convention is silently substituted for Equation 9. Candidate-set construction, Monte Carlo estimates and hyperparameter treatment also affect the practical score.

The displayed general GP mean on PDF p. 2 omits an explicit additive test mean, and the displayed prediction formulas do not explicitly include the observation-noise term introduced on p. 3. These expressions are not adopted as complete noisy, nonzero-mean prediction formulas. Singular covariance matrices, degenerate optimizer distributions and tied candidate values require explicit treatment beyond the usual no-tie Gaussian calculation.

The inspected main paper supports the mechanism and its stated settings. The two-page experimental supplement is dossier context rather than an additional mechanism evidence source. No author implementation, full optimizer, benchmark replication, convergence theorem, regret bound, universal speedup or globally optimal task-allocation policy is established by this record or the separate symbolic boundary assessment.

candidate_families.identity: AM changes reversible flow between two disjoint sets. NAM repeatedly applies structured AM steps using a focal value and a nested remaining set. These are construction families; the selection order gives named algorithms.

Section 8, p.28, DNAM order and UDNAM mixture
candidate_families.identity: UNAM uses nondecreasing conditional probabilities and is identified with Frigessi–Hwang–Younes (1992), independently Tjelmeland (2004). DNAM uses nonincreasing order. UDNAM is the equal UNAM/DNAM mixture.
candidate_families.next_work: Read original FHY/Tjelmeland sources for UNAM, full Sections 6–8 for DNAM, and decide whether UDNAM merits a separate identity. Do not attribute all three as original 2024 inventions.
candidate_families.limits: No universal ordering of UNAM and DNAM follows from lower self transitions. Ties and zero-support handling need explicit assessment.

locators: pp.35–36, eigenvalue argument and companion-theorem citation
candidate_families.identity: A named modification of DNAM that detects a step which would cause avoidable self transitions, then jointly handles the next two focal values and remaining tail. Its transition matrix can differ from DNAM; it is not an alias of Liu MHGS.
candidate_families.positive_evidence: The whole defining section and Algorithm 5 were read. Equation 91 presents a concrete distinction: the target (6,5,4,2,1)/18 gives a DNAM self probability 1/28 at the third state, while the ZDNAM example has no diagonal probability. The algorithm includes early handling for mass at least one half.
candidate_families.limits: The name does not promise zero self transitions when a conditional mass exceeds one half. Equation 95 supplies a counterexample to universal ZDNAM-over-DNAM efficiency domination. Source-reported eigenvalues 0.10306, -0.03639 and 0 were not recalculated here. The source efficiency-over-GS statement depends on reversible-kernel spectral theory and random variable selection; it is not a finite-run, systematic-scan or wall-clock guarantee.
next_work: Read full NAM/DNAM antecedents and the exact Neal–Rosenthal theorem version.
Check Algorithm 5 row sums, stationarity, detailed balance, zero tail, ties, point masses and the half-mass boundary with finite arithmetic.
Verify the illustrative transition entries and the counterexample before making calculated claims.
Curate a narrow local identity; assess AIO mapping afresh.

candidate_families.identity: ST shifts cumulative probability towers by the maximum probability and is attributed to Suwa–Todo (2010). HST uses a half-unit shift and is attributed to Suwa (2022). UST/DST choose opposite probability orders; UDST mixes them equally. OHST is an ordered HST variant.
candidate_families.next_work: Retrieve and read original Suwa sources. Distinguish an inherited construction, ordering convention and mixture algorithm before adding records. The report notes an ordering/formula convention issue in Suwa2022 in footnote18 on p.37; compare the original before implementing.
candidate_families.limits: Tower invariance and minimum-self properties do not establish general ergodicity or variance improvement. HST/OHST can be period-two and nonirreducible for uniform distributions with an even number of values (p.49). Implementation/pseudocode was read but not audited by execution.

locators: p.43, ZFSS reordering and boundary discussion
candidate_families.identity: A finite categorical conditional sampler which moves left at an auxiliary height through probability bars, after redistributing excess mass from the highest bar. ZFSS additionally reorders a qualifying blocker beside the highest bar to eliminate avoidable self transitions. The geometric redesign differs from the existing generic slice-sampling record and its interval stepping-out/doubling variants.
candidate_families.positive_evidence: The whole original method section and both algorithms were read. Figure10 was visually inspected: for probabilities (0.1,0.2,0.2,0.05,0.45), the illustrated current-maximum self probabilities are 5/9 for the simple left-slice construction, 1/9 for FSS and 0 for ZFSS. Those are source figures, not independent calculations in this handoff.
candidate_families.limits: FSS need not achieve minimum self probability; ZFSS does according to the section. The generic construction is nonreversible, but the dominant-mass boundary uses a reversible common kernel. Algorithms explicitly handle point masses, small state spaces and zero current mass. No asymptotic-variance or runtime ordering follows solely from self-transition reduction.
next_work: Decide whether to retain FSS and ZFSS separately with an explicit structural distinction or use a family-plus-variant treatment.
Check Algorithms 8–9 agree, including zero-probability current state, ties for maximum, m<=2, dominant mass>=1/2 and no-self regular cases.
Check finite stationarity, nonreversibility and invariant conditional-to-joint composition before curating.
Use the exact 2024 source identity and assess AIO mappings; do not alias generic SliceSampling.

shared_boundaries.assessment: If a conditional state has mass p>1/2, an invariant kernel must retain self probability at least (2p-1)/p there, giving minimum overall self mass 2p-1. At the half-mass boundary the named minimum-self constructions coincide in that special case; this does not make them globally identical.
Removing individual-coordinate self transitions does not ensure ergodicity of a composed sweep. The report gives a three-binary-variable scan example which fails to visit two of eight states.
Minimal self transitions are not a universal variance-optimality certificate. Separate reversibility, irreducibility, scan schedule, asymptotic-estimator and computation-cost assumptions.

shared_boundaries.locator: p.3 random-order discussion versus conclusion p.82
shared_boundaries.assessment: Use the nuanced scan discussion. Do not repeat a broad assertion that only independent random variable selection can yield a reversible overall algorithm; reversal-symmetric scan mixtures require separate treatment.

./reviews/structured/20261011T111426Z-population-and-density-methods/review.md:53:TPE is the particular two-density sequential optimizer introduced by Bergstra et al., not every Parzen density estimator, every expected-improvement method, Gaussian-process regression or the downstream Fast AutoAugment policy search that uses it. The quantile threshold groups observations for density fitting; it need not equal the best observed loss. Names and author order follow the inspected proceedings PDF. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 250 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in both worktree and main checkout, returning 9 lines in each checkout. These were references within neighboring records, their review and the prior discovery ledger, not records for the proposed identities. Fourteen exact AIO CLASS nodes with synonyms and outgoing edges and six neighboring native mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.

./reviews/structured/20261011T111426Z-population-and-density-methods/review.md:55:Represent valid configurations with a conditional generative tree so that some variables are active only for particular parent choices. Given observed configurations and losses to minimize, choose a loss threshold at a quantile gamma and fit l(x) from observations below that threshold and g(x) from the remainder. The model uses p(x|y)=l(x) below the threshold and g(x) otherwise, with p(x)=gamma*l(x)+(1−gamma)*g(x). Under this construction, expected nonnegative improvement E[max(y*−y,0)] is proportional, across configurations, to [gamma+(1−gamma)*g(x)/l(x)]^−1 wherever the relevant densities and expectation are defined. Draw candidate configurations from l, rank them by this expression, evaluate the selected candidate’s actual loss, and incorporate the observation into subsequent density estimates. The original estimator replaces continuous priors with adaptive Parzen mixtures around observed values and retains a prior component; bounded uniform variables use truncated Gaussian mixtures, log-uniform variables are modeled in log space, and categorical probabilities are reweighted by observed counts. The tree specifies conditional variable activation, not a decision tree that predicts loss. This is distinct from the separate Gaussian-process surrogate described in Section 3 of the same paper. Limits: The ratio ranking assumes the paper’s two-region conditional model and a finite, positive improvement constant. It is not the numerical value of expected improvement without that constant, nor an optimality or calibration guarantee. The derivation after Equation (3) prints an integral without the factor y in an expanded numerator. The unexpanded integral of (y*−y)*p(y) gives the density-ratio ranking recorded here. This is an explicit source qualification, not an author-issued erratum or a claim to reproduce a software implementation. The original tree-structured factorization encodes conditional activation and the specified density families. It does not establish arbitrary dependency modeling or identity with later multivariate TPE variants. Prior choices, density bandwidths, quantile selection, observations and finite candidate sampling affect search. No universal efficiency, final objective improvement or benchmark advantage is asserted.

./reviews/structured/20261011T115739Z-configuration-surrogates-and-evolution/review.md:47:Initialize with an evaluation of the default configuration, or a random setting when no default is available. Fit a random-forest surrogate using configuration values and, when available, training-instance features. Aggregate each tree’s predictions over instances according to the chosen cost metric, then derive predictive moments across trees. For runtime optimization the paper uses log-transformed responses while preserving the original aggregation objective through inverse transformation at leaves. Rank proposals by expected improvement, using its log-cost formulation, and search for promising settings with multistart one-coordinate local changes plus randomly sampled acquisition candidates. Interleave guided proposals with uniformly sampled configurations. The intensification routine compares a challenger and incumbent on shared instance/seed evaluations, enlarges the challenger’s evaluated subset in doubling batches, rejects it when its empirical cost is worse, and replaces the incumbent when the challenger has matched the available evaluation set and is at least as good. Repeat model fitting and configuration comparisons within the overall configuration budget. Limits: The original method explicitly lacks adaptive capping of individual poor runs. Its adaptive allocation of additional evaluations must not be equated with the censored-runtime handling or other features of later SMAC releases. Surrogate uncertainty and early empirical comparisons do not certify an optimal configuration or generalization to unseen instance distributions. The paper’s asymptotic argument assumes a finite configuration space, consistent cost estimates and unbounded evaluation growth; the displayed experimental procedure caps incumbent evaluations with maxR=2000. ./reviews/structured/20261011T111426Z-population-and-density-methods/review.md:55:Represent valid configurations with a conditional generative tree so that some variables are active only for particular parent choices. Given observed configurations and losses to minimize, choose a loss threshold at a quantile gamma and fit l(x) from observations below that threshold and g(x) from the remainder. The model uses p(x|y)=l(x) below the threshold and g(x) otherwise, with p(x)=gamma*l(x)+(1−gamma)*g(x). Under this construction, expected nonnegative improvement E[max(y*−y,0)] is proportional, across configurations, to [gamma+(1−gamma)*g(x)/l(x)]^−1 wherever the relevant densities and expectation are defined. Draw candidate configurations from l, rank them by this expression, evaluate the selected candidate’s actual loss, and incorporate the observation into subsequent density estimates. The original estimator replaces continuous priors with adaptive Parzen mixtures around observed values and retains a prior component; bounded uniform variables use truncated Gaussian mixtures, log-uniform variables are modeled in log space, and categorical probabilities are reweighted by observed counts. The tree specifies conditional variable activation, not a decision tree that predicts loss. This is distinct from the separate Gaussian-process surrogate described in Section 3 of the same paper. Limits: The ratio ranking assumes the paper’s two-region conditional model and a finite, positive improvement constant. It is not the numerical value of expected improvement without that constant, nor an optimality or calibration guarantee. The derivation after Equation (3) prints an integral without the factor y in an expanded numerator. The unexpanded integral of (y*−y)*p(y) gives the density-ratio ranking recorded here. This is an explicit source qualification, not an author-issued erratum or a claim to reproduce a software implementation. The original tree-structured factorization encodes conditional activation and the specified density families. It does not establish arbitrary dependency modeling or identity with later multivariate TPE variants. Prior choices, density bandwidths, quantile selection, observations and finite candidate sampling affect search. No universal efficiency, final objective improvement or benchmark advantage is asserted.

./reviews/structured/20261011T115739Z-configuration-surrogates-and-evolution/review.md:47:Initialize with an evaluation of the default configuration, or a random setting when no default is available. Fit a random-forest surrogate using configuration values and, when available, training-instance features. Aggregate each tree’s predictions over instances according to the chosen cost metric, then derive predictive moments across trees. For runtime optimization the paper uses log-transformed responses while preserving the original aggregation objective through inverse transformation at leaves. Rank proposals by expected improvement, using its log-cost formulation, and search for promising settings with multistart one-coordinate local changes plus randomly sampled acquisition candidates. Interleave guided proposals with uniformly sampled configurations. The intensification routine compares a challenger and incumbent on shared instance/seed evaluations, enlarges the challenger’s evaluated subset in doubling batches, rejects it when its empirical cost is worse, and replaces the incumbent when the challenger has matched the available evaluation set and is at least as good. Repeat model fitting and configuration comparisons within the overall configuration budget. Limits: The original method explicitly lacks adaptive capping of individual poor runs. Its adaptive allocation of additional evaluations must not be equated with the censored-runtime handling or other features of later SMAC releases. Surrogate uncertainty and early empirical comparisons do not certify an optimal configuration or generalization to unseen instance distributions. The paper’s asymptotic argument assumes a finite configuration space, consistent cost estimates and unbounded evaluation growth; the displayed experimental procedure caps incumbent evaluations with maxR=2000. These conditions are not an unconditional guarantee for the capped implementation or continuous spaces. Instance features are optional; the result is a single configuration and does not require test-instance feature computation. The reviewed source is an author-hosted manuscript, not a claim that its 15 PDF pages match the publisher’s page layout. No benchmark result or executable implementation was reproduced.

./reviews/structured/20261011T111426Z-population-and-density-methods/review.md:53:TPE is the particular two-density sequential optimizer introduced by Bergstra et al., not every Parzen density estimator, every expected-improvement method, Gaussian-process regression or the downstream Fast AutoAugment policy search that uses it. The quantile threshold groups observations for density fitting; it need not equal the best observed loss. Names and author order follow the inspected proceedings PDF. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 250 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in both worktree and main checkout, returning 9 lines in each checkout. These were references within neighboring records, their review and the prior discovery ledger, not records for the proposed identities. Fourteen exact AIO CLASS nodes with synonyms and outgoing edges and six neighboring native mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.

./reviews/structured/20261011T111426Z-population-and-density-methods/review.md:55:Represent valid configurations with a conditional generative tree so that some variables are active only for particular parent choices. Given observed configurations and losses to minimize, choose a loss threshold at a quantile gamma and fit l(x) from observations below that threshold and g(x) from the remainder. The model uses p(x|y)=l(x) below the threshold and g(x) otherwise, with p(x)=gamma*l(x)+(1−gamma)*g(x). Under this construction, expected nonnegative improvement E[max(y*−y,0)] is proportional, across configurations, to [gamma+(1−gamma)*g(x)/l(x)]^−1 wherever the relevant densities and expectation are defined. Draw candidate configurations from l, rank them by this expression, evaluate the selected candidate’s actual loss, and incorporate the observation into subsequent density estimates. The original estimator replaces continuous priors with adaptive Parzen mixtures around observed values and retains a prior component; bounded uniform variables use truncated Gaussian mixtures, log-uniform variables are modeled in log space, and categorical probabilities are reweighted by observed counts. The tree specifies conditional variable activation, not a decision tree that predicts loss. This is distinct from the separate Gaussian-process surrogate described in Section 3 of the same paper. Limits: The ratio ranking assumes the paper’s two-region conditional model and a finite, positive improvement constant. It is not the numerical value of expected improvement without that constant, nor an optimality or calibration guarantee. The derivation after Equation (3) prints an integral without the factor y in an expanded numerator. The unexpanded integral of (y*−y)*p(y) gives the density-ratio ranking recorded here. This is an explicit source qualification, not an author-issued erratum or a claim to reproduce a software implementation. The original tree-structured factorization encodes conditional activation and the specified density families. It does not establish arbitrary dependency modeling or identity with later multivariate TPE variants. Prior choices, density bandwidths, quantile selection, observations and finite candidate sampling affect search. No universal efficiency, final objective improvement or benchmark advantage is asserted.

No claim that their selected points differ on every problem is necessary.\\\",\\n    \\\"candidates\\\": [\\n      {\\n        \\\"id\\\": \\\"AIMech:EntropySearch\\\",\\n        \\\"name\\\": \\\"Entropy Search\\\",\\n        \\\"concept_kind\\\": \\\"algorithm\\\",\\n        \\\"aliases\\\": [],\\n        \\\"source_id\\\": \\\"hennig2012\\\",\\n        \\\"frontier_owner\\\": 176,\\n        \\\"proposed_scope\\\": \\\"The Hennig–Schuler2012 representer-point, EP and approximate expected-information-gain optimizer, rather than every information-based Bayesian optimization method.\\\",\\n        \\\"definition_for_assessment\\\": \\\"A Bayesian global optimization algorithm that represents the location of a function minimum on sampled representer points, approximates its probabilities with expectation propagation, and chooses evaluations using an approximate expected reduction in relative-entropy loss.\\\",\\n        \\\"mechanism\\\": [\\n          {\\n            \\\"claim\\\": \\\"Model a latent objective on a bounded continuous domain with a sufficiently regular GP and a specified observation likelihood; the core analytically tractable case is Gaussian observation noise. Infer a law for the minimizer rather than optimizing the posterior mean at every evaluation.\\\",\\n            \\\"locators\\\": \\\"Sections 1.1 and 2.1, PDF pp.2,5–7; Appendix A p.26.\\\"\\n          },\\n          {\\n            \\\"claim\\\": \\\"Sample finite representer points from a proposal with support across the domain, using PI/EI-shaped densities as proposed heuristics. The points are a quadrature representation; the next evaluation need not be one of them. Proposal values correct the nonuniform discrete loss, rather than replacing minimizer probabilities.\\\",\\n            \\\"locators\\\": \\\"Section 2.2 p.8; Section 2.5 p.13; Algorithm 1 p.19.\\\"\\n          },\\n          {\\n            \\\"claim\\\": \\\"For each representer point, use EP to approximate Gaussian inequality probabilities that it is the minimum; normalize/use the resulting finite probability representation and its derivatives with respect to the GP mean/covariance. This is approximate inference, not exact integration of the continuous optimizer law.\\\",\\n            \\\"locators\\\": \\\"Section 2.3 PDF pp.8–10; Algorithm 1 p.19.\\\"\\n          },\\n          {\\n            \\\"claim\\\": \\\"Use negative KL to a fixed uniform base as a loss. On the nonuniform discretization the varying part is H(q)-sum_i q_i log u_i, up to constants. This is more specific than entropy of the categorical weights alone.\\\",\\n            \\\"locators\\\": \\\"Section 2.5 PDF pp.12–13.\\\"\\n          },\\n          {\\n            \\\"claim\\\": \\\"Combine prospective GP mean/covariance innovations with an EP derivative expansion and fixed Monte Carlo innovation draws to approximate expected one-step loss change, then optimize this differentiable acquisition numerically and repeat after observation. The procedure is greedy, not optimal planning over the full remaining horizon.\\\",\\n            \\\"locators\\\": \\\"Sections 2.4,2.6–2.7 PDF pp.11,13–15; Algorithm 1 p.19.\\\"\\n          },\\n          {\\n            \\\"claim\\\": \\\"Hyperparameter learning is considered, with a proposed mixture-to-single-GP approximation, but the decision calculation does not include the full hierarchical learning process. PESC, parallel PES and max-value entropy methods are not automatic aliases or newly assessed leaves.\\\",\\n        \\\"definition_for_assessment\\\": \\\"A Bayesian global optimization algorithm that approximates information about the global maximizer by subtracting maximizer-conditioned predictive entropy from ordinary predictive entropy, using approximate maximizer samples and Gaussian constraint approximations.\\\",\\n        \\\"mechanism\\\": [\\n          {\\n            \\\"claim\\\": \\\"For fixed hyperparameters the target is information between the optimizer location and a future noisy evaluation. Mutual-information symmetry rewrites the same ideal optimizer-entropy reduction as predictive entropy minus expected predictive entropy conditioned on the optimizer. This is not simply maximizing predictive entropy.\\\",\\n            \\\"locators\\\": \\\"Main Section 2, PDF pp.2–3, Eqs.2–3.\\\"\\n          },\\n          {\\n            \\\"claim\\\": \\\"For a shift-invariant real kernel with a usable spectral distribution, draw random Fourier features and Gaussian posterior weights, optimize each resulting finite-feature sample function, and treat its maximizing location as an approximate posterior maximizer draw. Feature count and numerical maximization remain approximation choices.\\\",\\n            \\\"locators\\\": \\\"Main Section 2.1 p.3, Eq.5; Supplement A pp.1–2 / printed10–11.\\\"\\n          },\\n          {\\n            \\\"claim\\\": \\\"Approximate maximizer conditioning with zero-gradient/selected Hessian information, negative diagonal factors and a soft comparison with the largest noisy observation. Compute a Gaussian approximation using EP. The later sampled off-diagonal substitution does not make negative diagonals a general local-maximum certificate.\\\",\\n            \\\"locators\\\": \\\"Main Section 2.2 pp.4–5, Eqs.6–7; Supplement B.1–B.2 pp.2–3 / printed11–12.\\\"\\n          },\\n          {\\n            \\\"claim\\\": \\\"At candidate x impose f(x)<f(x_star) on a two-variable Gaussian approximation, obtain a truncated-normal variance, then approximate its marginal by a moment-matched Gaussian. Add the observation-noise variance before using the Gaussian entropy. The variance formula needs v=Var(f(x_star)-f(x))>0 and valid covariance; moments do not make the truncated law Gaussian.\\\",\\n            \\\"locators\\\": \\\"Main p.5, Eqs.8–9; Supplement B.3 pp.3–4 / printed12–13.\\\"\\n          },\\n          {\\n            \\\"claim\\\": \\\"Average the approximate variance-log differences over sampled GP hyperparameters and corresponding maximizer draws, with each noise variance belonging to its draw. Candidate-independent conditioning/EP terms can be reused. This is the source conditional-acquisition average, not a general identity for entropy under the fully marginalized model.\\\",\\n            \\\"locators\\\": \\\"Main Algorithm 2 p.2 and Section 2.3 p.5, Eq.10.\\\"\\n          },\\n          {\\n            \\\"claim\\\": \\\"Choose the next noisy evaluation by maximizing the approximate acquisition, update data and repeat. No claim that their selected points differ on every problem is necessary.\\\",\\n    \\\"candidates\\\": [\\n      {\\n        \\\"id\\\": \\\"AIMech:EntropySearch\\\",\\n        \\\"name\\\": \\\"Entropy Search\\\",\\n        \\\"concept_kind\\\": \\\"algorithm\\\",\\n        \\\"aliases\\\": [],\\n        \\\"source_id\\\": \\\"hennig2012\\\",\\n        \\\"frontier_owner\\\": 176,\\n        \\\"proposed_scope\\\": \\\"The Hennig–Schuler2012 representer-point, EP and approximate expected-information-gain optimizer, rather than every information-based Bayesian optimization method.\\\",\\n        \\\"definition_for_assessment\\\": \\\"A Bayesian global optimization algorithm that represents the location of a function minimum on sampled representer points, approximates its probabilities with expectation propagation, and chooses evaluations using an approximate expected reduction in relative-entropy loss.\\\",\\n        \\\"mechanism\\\": [\\n          {\\n            \\\"claim\\\": \\\"Model a latent objective on a bounded continuous domain with a sufficiently regular GP and a specified observation likelihood; the core analytically tractable case is Gaussian observation noise. Proposal values correct the nonuniform discrete loss, rather than replacing minimizer probabilities.\\\",\\n            \\\"locators\\\": \\\"Section 2.2 p.8; Section 2.5 p.13; Algorithm 1 p.19.\\\"\\n          },\\n          {\\n            \\\"claim\\\": \\\"For each representer point, use EP to approximate Gaussian inequality probabilities that it is the minimum; normalize/use the resulting finite probability representation and its derivatives with respect to the GP mean/covariance. Mutual-information symmetry rewrites the same ideal optimizer-entropy reduction as predictive entropy minus expected predictive entropy conditioned on the optimizer. This is not simply maximizing predictive entropy.\\\",\\n            \\\"locators\\\": \\\"Main Section 2, PDF pp.2–3, Eqs.2–3.\\\"\\n          },\\n          {\\n            \\\"claim\\\": \\\"For a shift-invariant real kernel with a usable spectral distribution, draw random Fourier features and Gaussian posterior weights, optimize each resulting finite-feature sample function, and treat its maximizing location as an approximate posterior maximizer draw. ./research/discovery/20261015T024219Z-predictive-entropy-search-with-constraints.json:48870:        "text": """"TEMP data-only PESC content for root assessment; never invoked here.

Required sources: hernandez2015 (official ICML/PMLR main, nine pages),
hernandez2015-supplement (official nine-page supplement), and hernandez2016
(official JMLR expanded report; only pages 1–3, 12–22 and 41–49 inspected).
The scope is the core constrained-optimizer acquisition, not PESC-F or the
general resource scheduler. Source equation caveats remain explicit; this
module does not certify a repaired EP implementation. The future
research/discovery/pesc-boundaries.py refers to the frozen original bounded
diagnostics and actual execution receipts, not author code or a GP benchmark.
Existing PES frontier owner 177 is contextual, not an existing PESC owner.
"""


def content(now, snapshot, sources, identity):
    def ev(locator, source='hernandez2015'):
        return dict(source_id=source, locator=locator, relation='supports')

    def claim(key, kind, statement, locator, extra=None):
        evidence = [ev(locator)]
        if extra is not None:
            evidence.append(extra)
        return dict(claim_id=key, kind=kind, statement=statement, evidence=evidence)

    return dict(
        id='AIMech:PredictiveEntropySearchWithConstraints',
        name='Predictive Entropy Search with Constraints',
        concept_kind='algorithm',
        definition=(
            'A Bayesian optimization algorithm for an unknown objective and '
            'unknown inequality constraints that selects evaluations using '
            'an approximation to information about the constrained minimizer '
            'location, combining posterior optimizer samples, finite '
            'feasibility and optimality indicators, Gaussian expectation '
            'propagation and taskwise predictive observation entropies.'
        ),
        definition_evidence=[ev('Section 3, PDF pp. 3–5, Equations 6–16')],
        claims=[
            claim(
                'constrained-optimizer-information-target', 'mechanism',
                'The problem minimizes f(x) subject to c_k(x)>=0 for '
                'each constraint, with objective and constraints defined '
                'throughout the search domain. Assume posterior function '
                'draws have an attained feasible minimum and an almost '
                'surely unique minimizer or a specified measurable tie '
                'selection. At fixed data and model hyperparameters, the '
                'ideal acquisition targets I(X_star;Y|D,x), where X_star '
                'is that constrained minimizer location and Y contains '
                'the prospective objective and constraint observations. '
                'When the entropy terms are well-defined, this equals '
                'H(Y|D,x)-E_X_star[H(Y|D,x,X_star)]. The acquisition does '
                'not require an already observed feasible incumbent. '
                'That property does not specify how to handle a posterior '
                'function draw with no feasible point or no attained minimum.',
                'PDF p. 1, Equation 1 and introductory motivation; '
                'Section 3, PDF p. 3, Equations 6–7',
                extra=ev('Section 4, PDF p. 13, Equations 7–8 and '
                         'the optimizer sampling definition', 'hernandez2016'),
            ),
            claim(
                'approximate-constrained-optimizer-sampling', 'mechanism',
                'The practical method models the objective and constraints '
                'with independent Gaussian processes and independent '
                'Gaussian observation noise. It approximates the '
                'expectation over X_star with a finite average: draw '
                'approximate posterior functions and numerically minimize '
                'the sampled objective under the sampled constraints. '
                'The described sampler uses a finite basis approximation '
                'for stationary covariance functions, so the generated '
                'optimizer samples are approximate. Sampling GP '
                'hyperparameters and averaging their acquisition scores '
                'is an additional approximation, not in general the '
                'information obtained by first marginalizing predictive '
                'distributions over hyperparameters. The source does not '
                'guarantee that its numerical searches find every global '
                'optimizer.',
                'Section 3, PDF p. 3, model assumptions and paragraph '
                'following Equation 8',
                extra=ev('Sections 4.1, 4.3 and 4.6, PDF pp. 14, 20–22, '
                         'Equation 21; Appendix B.3, PDF p. 49',
                         'hernandez2016'),
            ),
            claim(
                'finite-feasibility-and-optimality-indicators', 'mechanism',
                'For a proposed optimizer x_star, define '
                'Gamma(z)=product_k 1[c_k(z)>=0] and '
                'Psi(z)=Gamma(z)*1[f(z)>=f(x_star)]+1-Gamma(z). '
                'Gamma(x_star) requires feasibility and Psi(z) excludes '
                'a feasible point with strictly smaller objective value. '
                'The method replaces the domain-wide product of Psi '
                'factors with a finite collection at observed inputs '
                'and the candidate, with x_star also represented in the '
                'latent Gaussian variables. This finite restriction is '
                'not exact global optimality conditioning. Even on a '
                'finite domain the indicators express membership in '
                'the minimizer set, not a normalized optimizer density '
                'or a rule selecting one tied minimizer. Equality '
                'c_k(z)=0 is feasible under the source step convention.',
                'Section 3, PDF pp. 4–5, Equations 9–15; original '
                '81-case finite indicator diagnostic in '
                'research/discovery/pesc-boundaries.py',
                extra=ev('Section 4.2, PDF pp. 16–19, Equations 15–20; '
                         'Section 4.6, PDF p. 21', 'hernandez2016'),
            ),
            claim(
                'factorized-ep-and-candidate-moments', 'mechanism',
                'Expectation propagation replaces the finite non-Gaussian '
                'feasibility and optimality factors with Gaussian sites. '
                'The resulting approximation factorizes between the '
                'objective and constraint functions while retaining '
                'covariances between represented values of each function. '
                'The calculation separates the observed-input and '

./research/discovery/20261015T032623Z-pesc-f.json:25547:            "./research/discovery/20261015T024219Z-predictive-entropy-search-with-constraints.json:49285:        \"text\": \"{\\n  \\\"id\\\": \\\"AIMech:PredictiveEntropySearchWithConstraints\\\",\\n  \\\"name\\\": \\\"Predictive Entropy Search with Constraints\\\",\\n  \\\"concept_kind\\\": \\\"algorithm\\\",\\n  \\\"definition\\\": \\\"A Bayesian optimization algorithm for an unknown objective and unknown inequality constraints that selects evaluations using an approximation to information about the constrained minimizer location, combining posterior optimizer samples, finite feasibility and optimality indicators, Gaussian expectation propagation and taskwise predictive observation entropies.\\\",\\n  \\\"definition_evidence\\\": [\\n    {\\n      \\\"source_id\\\": \\\"hernandez2015\\\",\\n      \\\"locator\\\": \\\"Section 3, PDF pp. 3\\\\u20135, Equations 6\\\\u201316\\\",\\n      \\\"relation\\\": \\\"supports\\\"\\n    }\\n  ],\\n  \\\"claims\\\": [\\n    {\\n      \\\"claim_id\\\": \\\"constrained-optimizer-information-target\\\",\\n      \\\"kind\\\": \\\"mechanism\\\",\\n      \\\"statement\\\": \\\"The problem minimizes f(x) subject to c_k(x)>=0 for each constraint, with objective and constraints defined throughout the search domain. Assume posterior function draws have an attained feasible minimum and an almost surely unique minimizer or a specified measurable tie selection. At fixed data and model hyperparameters, the ideal acquisition targets I(X_star;Y|D,x), where X_star is that constrained minimizer location and Y contains the prospective objective and constraint observations. When the entropy terms are well-defined, this equals H(Y|D,x)-E_X_star[H(Y|D,x,X_star)]. The acquisition does not require an already observed feasible incumbent. That property does not specify how to handle a posterior function draw with no feasible point or no attained minimum.\\\",\\n      \\\"evidence\\\": [\\n        {\\n          \\\"source_id\\\": \\\"hernandez2015\\\",\\n          \\\"locator\\\": \\\"PDF p. 1, Equation 1 and introductory motivation; Section 3, PDF p. 3, Equations 6\\\\u20137\\\",\\n          \\\"relation\\\": \\\"supports\\\"\\n        },\\n        {\\n          \\\"source_id\\\": \\\"hernandez2016\\\",\\n          \\\"locator\\\": \\\"Section 4, PDF p. 13, Equations 7\\\\u20138 and the optimizer sampling definition\\\",\\n          \\\"relation\\\": \\\"supports\\\"\\n        }\\n      ]\\n    },\\n    {\\n      \\\"claim_id\\\": \\\"approximate-constrained-optimizer-sampling\\\",\\n      \\\"kind\\\": \\\"mechanism\\\",\\n      \\\"statement\\\": \\\"The practical method models the objective and constraints with independent Gaussian processes and independent Gaussian observation noise. ./reviews/structured/20261011T111426Z-population-and-density-methods/review.md:53:TPE is the particular two-density sequential optimizer introduced by Bergstra et al., not every Parzen density estimator, every expected-improvement method, Gaussian-process regression or the downstream Fast AutoAugment policy search that uses it. ./reviews/structured/20261011T111426Z-population-and-density-methods/review.md:55:Represent valid configurations with a conditional generative tree so that some variables are active only for particular parent choices. Given observed configurations and losses to minimize, choose a loss threshold at a quantile gamma and fit l(x) from observations below that threshold and g(x) from the remainder. The model uses p(x|y)=l(x) below the threshold and g(x) otherwise, with p(x)=gamma*l(x)+(1−gamma)*g(x). Under this construction, expected nonnegative improvement E[max(y*−y,0)] is proportional, across configurations, to [gamma+(1−gamma)*g(x)/l(x)]^−1 wherever the relevant densities and expectation are defined. Draw candidate configurations from l, rank them by this expression, evaluate the selected candidate’s actual loss, and incorporate the observation into subsequent density estimates. The original estimator replaces continuous priors with adaptive Parzen mixtures around observed values and retains a prior component; bounded uniform variables use truncated Gaussian mixtures, log-uniform variables are modeled in log space, and categorical probabilities are reweighted by observed counts. The tree specifies conditional variable activation, not a decision tree that predicts loss. This is distinct from the separate Gaussian-process surrogate described in Section 3 of the same paper. Limits: The ratio ranking assumes the paper’s two-region conditional model and a finite, positive improvement constant. It is not the numerical value of expected improvement without that constant, nor an optimality or calibration guarantee. The derivation after Equation (3) prints an integral without the factor y in an expanded numerator. The unexpanded integral of (y*−y)*p(y) gives the density-ratio ranking recorded here. This is an explicit source qualification, not an author-issued erratum or a claim to reproduce a software implementation. The original tree-structured factorization encodes conditional activation and the specified density families. It does not establish arbitrary dependency modeling or identity with later multivariate TPE variants. Prior choices, density bandwidths, quantile selection, observations and finite candidate sampling affect search. No universal efficiency, final objective improvement or benchmark advantage is asserted.

./reviews/structured/20261011T115739Z-configuration-surrogates-and-evolution/review.md:47:Initialize with an evaluation of the default configuration, or a random setting when no default is available. Fit a random-forest surrogate using configuration values and, when available, training-instance features. Aggregate each tree’s predictions over instances according to the chosen cost metric, then derive predictive moments across trees. For runtime optimization the paper uses log-transformed responses while preserving the original aggregation objective through inverse transformation at leaves. Rank proposals by expected improvement, using its log-cost formulation, and search for promising settings with multistart one-coordinate local changes plus randomly sampled acquisition candidates. Interleave guided proposals with uniformly sampled configurations. The intensification routine compares a challenger and incumbent on shared instance/seed evaluations, enlarges the challenger’s evaluated subset in doubling batches, rejects it when its empirical cost is worse, and replaces the incumbent when the challenger has matched the available evaluation set and is at least as good. Repeat model fitting and configuration comparisons within the overall configuration budget. Limits: The original method explicitly lacks adaptive capping of individual poor runs. Its adaptive allocation of additional evaluations must not be equated with the censored-runtime handling or other features of later SMAC releases. Surrogate uncertainty and early empirical comparisons do not certify an optimal configuration or generalization to unseen instance distributions. The paper’s asymptotic argument assumes a finite configuration space, consistent cost estimates and unbounded evaluation growth; the displayed experimental procedure caps incumbent evaluations with maxR=2000.
